articles.title: Truce begins in Ukrainian city of Oleshky after it was announced by Melania Trump
articles.summary: The ceasefire is meant to allow aid deliveries and the evacuation of civilians.
articles.body:
A truce has begun in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, a week after it was announced by US First Lady, Melania Trump.

The ceasefire is meant to allow aid deliveries and the evacuation of civilians.

Russia's defence ministry said on Telegram it had stopped firing toward the Ukrainian city of Kherson - across the river from Oleshky - at 04:00 Moscow time (01:00 GMT) in preparation for the humanitarian operation.

Oleshky is on the south bank of the river Dnipro, which forms the front line in the Kherson region. The remaining residents have been desperately short of food and other essential supplies.

White House says Melania Trump brokered truce for Ukraine city 'on brink of disaster'

Ukraine's parliament commissioner for human rights, Dmytro Lubinets, confirmed in a social media post that the ceasefire had begun.

"As head of the Ukrainian negotiating team, I confirm that the Ukrainian side is honouring its commitments," he wrote on Facebook.

Oleshky was seized by Russia during the first days of its full-scale invasion in February 2022.

Residents were trapped with scarce food between Ukrainian positions across the Dnipro River and Russian forces to the east.

The city was home to 24,000 people before the war. Now Ukraine estimates that some 6,000 people remain in the city and its surrounding areas, including 200 children.

The White House said last week that Melania Trump had secured the ceasefire in Oleshky.

"Non-military, civilian leaders from both countries will work together to visit Oleshky residents in their homes and determine the level of assistance they require," she said in a press release.

While the US first lady is relatively lower profile than some of her predecessors - and only occasionally seen at White House events - she has become involved in addressing humanitarian issues stemming from the Russia-Ukraine war.

In August 2025, she penned a letter to Putin, telling him it was "time to protect children and future generations worldwide".

articles.title: Judge further extends block on Trump administration’s removing trees at D.C. golf course
articles.summary: The judge noted that the president’s social media posts contradicted multiple government officials’ sworn testimony.
articles.body: A federal judge in Washington issued a longer-term injunction Monday blocking the Trump administration from removing or damaging any additional trees on the grounds of East Potomac Golf Links. The order says the administration must provide written notice 10 business days before it makes “any irreparable modification to any forms or features of East Potomac Park” while the case proceeds. In her order, U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes cited some of President Donald Trump’s Truth Social posts, which contradicted testimony from government employees. “This started as a case about golf. That good walk spoiled. But it has become much more. It now forces the Court to reconcile assertions by President Donald J. Trump with the sworn testimony of multiple government employees and the argument of senior Department of Justice attorneys,” Reyes wrote. The order displayed screenshots of Truth Social posts, including one on Oct. 18 in which Trump said Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, along with an architect, had “developed a plan to build a World Class Championship Golf Course” at East Potomac starting Nov. 15, even though Justice Department lawyers had earlier said there was no renovation plan. In a follow-up post Oct. 19, Trump said work on the course would begin not on Nov. 15, but “IMMEDIATELY!” That post also said workers did not need approval for construction and called Reyes “a crazed lunatic.” “Rarely, if ever, has the United States Department of Justice urged a federal court not to believe the sitting President,” Reyes wrote in her order Monday. “And yet, here we are.” Reyes said during a seven-hour hearing this month that she believed it was most likely necessary to extend her order pausing the tree demolition because she had already found the government acted in “bad faith” when it abruptly chopped down more than 400 trees at the course over the Columbus Day holiday weekend. “The Court earlier stated, ‘I am not the Lorax. I do not speak for the trees.’ The Court still does not speak for the trees. It speaks only for the rule of law,” Reyes wrote Monday. Democracy Forward President and CEO Skye Perryman, who is representing plaintiffs in the case, praised Monday’s ruling in a statement. “This is a big win that will rightly protect East Potomac park from further irreparable harm,” Perryman said. “We are grateful the court intervened to stop the Trump-Vance association’s greed and lawlessness while the case continues, and we are eager to argue the case in court.”

articles.title: US midterm elections: Trump's biggest economic problem looks familiar
articles.summary: Donald Trump heads into the US midterm elections with an issue similar to his political foe Joe Biden.
articles.body:
The White House is confronting a familiar dilemma. The economic numbers aren't necessarily bad - but the public mood is.

It's a disconnect that haunted Joe Biden in 2024, when solid headline data failed to convince many voters that the economy was working for them.

Now, Donald Trump faces a version of the same challenge.

During the 2024 campaign, Trump promised voters swift relief from rising prices.

"When I win, I will immediately bring prices down," he said.

Delivering on that promise has proved harder than expected.

Economic growth is holding up, unemployment remains low and the stock market is near record highs.

Yet the final inflation report ahead of the midterm elections confirms what voters already know: prices remain high .

The causes are different. Biden was grappling with the aftermath of the Covid pandemic. Trump faces higher energy prices linked to the US-Israel conflict with Iran and the fallout from some of his own trade and immigration policies.

The political reality, however, is much the same. Voters are not judging the economy by GDP figures or record highs on the stock market. They are judging it by what they pay at the supermarket, petrol prices and whether they can keep up with the bills.

US economic growth of 2.2% would be respectable by the standards of many wealthy economies. Germany, for example, has struggled to generate comparable momentum. And a stable US unemployment rate of 4.2% hardly suggests an economy in freefall.

Trump argues that he inherited an economic mess from Biden, and points to strong growth, investment and stock market performance as evidence that his policies are working.

Following the most recent inflation report, White House spokesman Matthew Middleton said the administration's "aggressive, pro-growth economic agenda" had blunted "Biden's inflation crisis".

Larry Kudlow, a Trump ally and economic commentator, has described the current expansion as "the greatest story never told" , arguing that "nobody is getting fired".

US inflation rises more than expected - here's what is happening with prices

But voters appear to be reading a different story - one in which Trump won the presidency promising to tackle the cost of living, only for prices to keep rising.

Part of the problem is that wage increases have not kept pace with prices. Average hourly earnings have risen 3% over the last year, while consumer prices have increased 3.7%.

That helps explain why polls continue to show voters giving Trump poor marks for his handling of the economy.

For Democrats, the dynamic feels familiar.

Celinda Lake, a veteran Democratic pollster, says the problem begins with the way economists and voters use the same language to mean different things.

"When economists say inflation comes down, they mean the rate of increase has come down," she says.

"When voters say inflation has come down, they mean the price has returned to what it was. Well, of course, it never returns to what it was."

The Biden administration spent much of 2024 highlighting low unemployment, solid growth and falling inflation. However, many voters remained focused on the higher prices they faced every day.

Lake, who advised Biden's 2020 campaign but was not involved in the 2024 race, says voters judge the economy through personal experience, not economic indicators.

"You can't argue with people about their own lived reality," she says.

That may help explain why Trump's challenge looks so similar to Biden's.

Biden's critics blamed him for inflation. But he could point to forces largely outside his control, including the pandemic and its supply chain aftershocks.

Some economists argue that today's higher prices are at least partly the result of his own policies, including tariffs, as well as the economic fallout from the US-Israel war with Iran.

"The inflation is clearly traceable to Donald Trump," says Peter Morici, a University of Maryland economist who aligns with Republicans.

"It's his tariffs and the war. People know that. They see it."

Trump's "Liberation Day" tariffs, announced in April 2025, have added to costs for consumers.

A study by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York found the tariffs increased consumer goods prices by about 2.9%.

The impact might have been larger if Trump hadn't later paused some tariffs, struck new trade deals and been blocked by the Supreme Court from using emergency powers to impose many others.

Then came another shock. Conflict with Iran pushed oil prices higher, lifting the cost of petrol and putting fresh pressure on household budgets.

The White House points to tax cuts, job growth and lower prescription drug costs as evidence that the administration is delivering for American families. And it is increasingly embracing policies aimed at easing pressures.

Trump has called for a cap on credit card interest rates and floated the idea of a $5,000 payment to American adults if Republicans retain control of Congress.

The measures reflect a political reality familiar to both parties: when voters are anxious about prices, arguments about solid growth and low unemployment are rarely enough.

Biden never found a way to bridge the gap between economic performance and economic sentiment. The question heading into the midterms is whether Trump can.

If recent political history is any guide, perceptions of the economy may matter more than the economic data itself.

articles.title: ‘They wanted my voice gone’: A swing-seat, pro-Israel Democrat is fending off criticism from both parties
articles.summary: Jared Moskowitz’s race in Florida is a referendum on whether a loudly pro-Israel and adamant denouncer of antisemitism fits anymore in the Democratic Party.
articles.body:
A week before the Israeli elections that will determine Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's future, the only two Jewish candidates running against each other to represent one of the most heavily Jewish House districts in the country met for their first face-to-face at a synagogue the name of which literally translates to "children of Israel" — referring to the people, not the country.

Attendees needed to provide their license plates in advance and bring photo identification to get in the door, passing through a body scanner. Armed and unarmed guards were positioned through the building. Rep. Jared Moskowitz, the Democrat who'd be considered a progressive on most other issues beyond Israel, and former Boca Raton Mayor Scott Singer, his Republican challenger, each entered with two large security guards who stood the whole time just to the side of the stage. The hour-long forum went 28 minutes before a question that wasn't about Israel and antisemitism.

The race, the synagogue's interim rabbi Cy Stanway told CNN after listening to the forum, is a "bellwether" — on support for Israel, antisemitism, Jews running against each other … he was still ticking through significances as congregants interrupted to share their own takes on what the race represents.

It's also a referendum on Moskowitz, and whether a loudly pro-Israel and adamant denouncer of antisemitism fits anymore in the Democratic Party.

The answer to that question will resonate far beyond South Florida, as multiple Jewish candidates are gearing up to launch 2028 presidential campaigns at the same moment that condemning Israel is emerging as a clear litmus test for the Democratic primaries.

For decades, American Jews were one of the most supportive and consistent Democratic constituencies. But the October 7 attacks , President Donald Trump's hardline support for Israel and the spread of anti-Israel sentiment among some Democrats have ripped them apart politically in ways that are all playing out in this House race.

By Republicans, American Jews are being told to stomach antisemitism coursing past the conservative fringes and Trump's embrace of a prime minister deeply unpopular among them. By Democrats, they're being told to subjugate their concerns to the larger fight for majorities in Congress, to listen to former President Barack Obama at an event in Belfast this month say Israelis "took land off people, and they were excessive," to accept New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani going from outlier to trendsetter as anti-Zionism becomes de rigueur and antisemitism gets minimized.

"If you don't want to be with the Democrats as a whole because you feel that way, I understand," Moskowitz told CNN in an interview. "But in this race, that's not the case."

"The reason why the Jewish community is so on edge is because the beginning of those stories of our grandparents are starting to come true again," Moskowitz said. "We're being blamed for things we have nothing to do with. The conspiracy theories are out of control. If Hitler had TikTok, I don't know that the Jews would have survived, and America might be speaking German."

This is the rare race where the Democrat brags about being the one with AIPAC's endorsement and embraces being grouped in with renegade Democratic Pennsylvania Sen. John Fetterman on Israel.

Two days before the forum, Moskowitz sat by the large rusting pink flamingo in the back patio of the Ole Ole Steakhouse in Miami Beach, being offered tray after tray of croquettes and flatbreads, a few minutes before he closed out a Latino supporter event by calling out the winning ticket numbers for a raffle of new cookware pieces — "I was born for this moment," he joked. Moskowitz told CNN that while his main job if he returns to Washington will be tackling the affordability crisis he hears about across every demographic in the district, he now has a larger mission.

Police are permanently stationed outside Moskowitz's home after a man with an antisemitic manifesto was arrested for targeting him for assassination. Another man was arrested just last week for threatening his life.

Put that together with a Democratic Socialists of America primary challenger who ran against him because of his Israel views and was embraced by likeminded advocates around the country, Moskowitz said, and he's digging in.

"They wanted my voice gone. That voice is not only not going anywhere, that voice is now pissed," Moskowitz said. "These people need economic help. They absolutely need economic help, but this litmus test that all of a sudden is breeding in the Democratic Party that you've got to be anti- our number one ally, or you've got to say things like, 'It's a genocide,' which is a blood libel against Jews in this country and which is making us less safe? Yeah, I'm going to fight that wherever it is."

What Moskowitz means for Hakeem Jeffries

This is just one House seat amid a battle for the majority that's playing out in districts red, blue and purple across the country. But because of his antics aimed for the cameras at committee hearings, the proudly impish 45-year-old Moskowitz quickly became one of the best-known junior members of Congress in the country.

Republicans in Tallahassee and DC came up with a plan: as part of their own rushed off-cycle redistricting, they redrew the district to one where Trump won by 9 points in 2024, recruited the well-known but elected as a non-partisan Jewish mayor of one of the best-known cities in it, then poured in millions. Singer, with his South Florida perma-tan and hair spray keeping his gray comb-up perfectly in place, looked the part.

It's the most expensive House race in America — well over $40 million in cumulative spending already, and expected to edge at least past $50 million in the final days. Ads are running non-stop, full of too many claims and fudged phrases for anyone to make sense of. Signs are hooked onto the fences of condos and at intersections. Voters are having to divine which district they live in post-gerrymandering by sorting through all the brochures swamping their mailboxes.

Now that the race is almost done, Moskowitz says he has told House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries he feels a little guilty with how much cash is being poured into him while multiple other races on the cusp in Florida and beyond could be shifted by a fraction of it.

But Moskowitz and Democrats in DC like that he's also sucking up money that Republicans weren't planning to spend there. To Jeffries, a person familiar with the leader's thinking tells CNN, this and other races where he could buck GOP efforts to redistrict Democrats out of reach of the majority were "personal."

In another measure of how fraught Israel has become for Democrats, Israel critics like former Obama deputy national security adviser Ben Rhodes and several incoming DSA House members blasted Jeffries for betraying party voters for appointing Moskowitz the ranking member on the Middle East and North Africa Subcommittee. The truth is, even though Moskowitz thanked the leader for the job, Jeffries wasn't directly involved.

California Rep. Brad Sherman, who was up for it, decided giving it over to Moskowitz would help in his House race, but also in much bigger ways.

"That he'll be chair of that subcommittee," Sherman told CNN by phone, "is significant to everyone who wants a reasonable and balanced policy in the Middle East."

Meanwhile, at the top of his ticket Moskowitz has Angie Nixon, a former state legislator who joined the DSA to run for Senate and has leaned into claims that Israel has committed genocide, though he said he was too focused on his race to have an opinion on her, but was glad to point out that he hasn't campaigned with her.

The race isn't all coming down to Jews and Israel. The new district, which runs along the coast roughly from Delray Beach to Miami Beach, also has a big Latino population, and Ileana Martinez, who's been organizing for Republicans many of the years since she first arrived from Colombia in 1979, was eager to put together the steakhouse event for Moskowitz. She and some other Latinos who supported the president in 2024 now feel "we are on a very disgusting thing with Trump."

But in an interview in an office just off the synagogue's sanctuary shortly after the forum, Singer told CNN that the overall affluence of the district has meant less stress on affordability than elsewhere, and more time for the race to focus on Democrats' changing views on Israel and socialism.

In signs around the district and a dozen times on stage at the forum, the Republican tied Moskowitz to Minnesota Rep. Ilhan Omar, the strongly anti-Israel Minnesota congresswoman from the Squad who in a much different political moment back in 2019 — before Moskowitz was in Congress — had to apologize for a post claiming support for Israel was all about money in what was widely condemned as an antisemitic trope.

"People who understand that support for Israel and standing up to antisemitism are key issues will find an easier home in the Republican Party or an easier voting with someone who will stand up to those issues and not empower people like Ilhan Omar as my opponent did," Singer charged.

The difference between Republicans and Democrats, Singer charged, is that the anti-Israel and antisemitic forces on the right are mostly podcasters and not elected officials. On stage during the forum, he had shrugged off Trump's use of "shylock" at a Kansas rally last week in describing people who chase more money than they're owed as "an ill-advised term," but one that has "multiple meanings."

"Merchant of Venice," Singer said, happens to be his favorite Shakespeare play. Asked in the interview if "Shylock" is an antisemitic term, Singer said, "it's often used that way, yes."

Asked if he could point to an example outside of a production of "The Merchant of Venice" when it wasn't used in an antisemitic way, Singer said, "just as a lender. I remember the movie 'Get Shorty,' John Travolta used it."

Anyway, Singer said, he's more focused on what Trump has done standing by Israel and appointing envoys to fight antisemitism.

Singer and Moskowitz both insist the only election they're focused on is theirs — but they can't help looking over to Israel's and wondering what it will mean for the fight that's playing out in Florida and beyond.

Netanyahu, Singer said, has been "a transformative leader."

Moskowitz has been more critical of Netanyahu but says he doesn't think the fight he's having is going to be changed much by whoever emerges as the next prime minister.

"Ultimately, Israel could use a new face of the country. It's not going to, by the way, fundamentally change what's happening on the far left and in DSA," he said. "But it will provide maybe a breath to recalibrate here on Israel's future."

articles.title: LIZ PEEK: Five reasons Republicans could defy the polls and shock Democrats on Election Day
articles.summary: With Election Day one week away, Abdul El-Sayed's Michigan Senate race against Mike Rogers tightens as polls face scrutiny across the board.
articles.body: Election Day is one week away. Most pundits are ready to declare the midterms over and Democrats the victors. But hold on: There are several reasons Republicans may outperform the gloomy polls and forecasts making headlines. First, Democrats are unpopular. A recent CNN poll showed Democratic favorability at 35%, considerably below the 38% awarded President Trump in the most recent RealClearPolling average. Second, Republicans are flush with campaign cash that is now flowing into tough races across the country. Money doesn’t win elections (see: Kamala Harris), but it can help snag undecided voters. That is true especially in contests like the Michigan Senate race, where little-known Democrat Abdul El-Sayed is facing off against Mike Rogers, a veteran and moderate GOP former congressman. Voters are just now discovering allegations about El-Sayed’s possible family ties to the designated terrorist group, the Muslim Brotherhood, causing the polls to tighten. Fox News recently reported, "El-Sayed has also faced scrutiny over social media posts from his half-sister describing their mother's alleged involvement in Muslim Brotherhood activism in the 1970s. He has denied personal or family ties to the organization and said he was raised by his father and stepmother." ABDUL EL-SAYED'S ALLEGED FAMILY TIES TO MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD SURFACE AFTER DENYING ANY LINK DURING NBC INTERVIEW Third, President Trump is campaigning vigorously, reminding voters why they elected him. Given the incessant attacks on the commander in chief by the liberal media, his rallies are essential. Yes, his approval numbers have been weighed down by the Iran war, but his appearances will help drive turnout. Fourth, the far left overwhelmed primaries earlier this year, causing Democrats to put up some controversial candidates, like Senate hopefuls James Talarico in Texas and Troy Jackson in Maine. LIZ PEEK: A BLUE WAVE? THE LIBERAL MEDIA WANTS ONE, BUT VOTERS MIGHT DISAGREE Fifth, to quote a recent piece in The Economist: "The polls could be wrong." While the publication concludes that polling errors at the national level have, in different elections, overcounted both Republicans and Democrats, when it comes to specific states and districts, the goofs follow "a remarkably consistent pattern." In the current races, The Economist writes, "applying the historical trend to this year’s polls reverses Democratic leads in the pivotal states of Alaska and Texas. In Ohio, the Democratic advantage would be cut to less than one percentage point, while Iowa and Kansas would move from being tied to leaning Republican." LEE CARTER: POLLS SAY DEMOCRATS COULD SWAMP REPUBLICANS. AS A POLLSTER, I HAVE A QUESTION CNN reported the same thing a few nights ago, with analyst Harry Enten describing Democrats’ lead in numerous toss-up states as "nominal" and pointing out that polling in states won by Trump in the past has undercounted Republicans by more than 4 points. If that same level of error persists, the GOP will win in Texas, Maine, Iowa and Kansas, and keep the Senate. In this year’s election cycle, polling has come under even more scrutiny than usual, especially as totally made-up surveys have entered the mix and been included in supposedly sophisticated aggregates like those published by The New York Times and FiftyPlusOne, which helped reveal the frauds. An outfit called Wedgewood Polls admitted that it had fabricated polls as an "experiment." Some have alleged the fake surveys were meant to boost far-left candidates like Wisconsin gubernatorial hopeful Francesca Hong, while others have insinuated that the originators of the Wedgewood polls were using betting sites to benefit from the fallout. DEMOCRATS FURIOUS AFTER POLLSTER BOOSTING FAR-LEFT CANDIDATES ADMITS FABRICATING SURVEYS: ‘ABSOLUTE SCUMBAGS’ Wedgewood isn’t alone; several other survey organizations, including Median Strategies and Public Sentiment Institute, have also been revealed as dishonest or out-and-out frauds. Whatever confidence people had in the polling industry has deflated like a Hillary Clinton election-night balloon. Remember that most media outlets are rooting for Democrats to take over Congress and punish President Trump. Publishing stories and polls that present the election as essentially over is calculated. If it suppresses GOP turnout and campaign donations in close races, so much the better. DEMOCRATS THINK A BLUE WAVE IS BUILDING. HERE ARE 3 FORCES THAT COULD STOP IT No one should be driven by polls or gloomy headlines. Instead, consider which candidate is offering policies that history shows lead to better outcomes: lower taxes, lighter regulations that reduce costs, robust law enforcement that produces safer communities, strict oversight of welfare spending that reduces fraud and enables assistance for those who need it, and rigorous education. Those are the policies that have made Florida more successful than New York and Texas more appealing than California. Policies matter. OBAMA PREPARES TO RALLY WITH MICHIGAN DEM WHO ONCE DELIVERED SCATHING VERDICT ON HIS PRESIDENCY Voters should also ignore Democratic race-baiting. When President Obama, campaigning in Michigan with Sen. Elissa Slotkin for Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, said, "Imagine the power duo of Abdul and Elissa. You got a Muslim man, a Jewish woman, fighting for you in the U.S. Senate. That’s something, Michigan, you can be proud of." That’s vintage Obama, slicing and dicing our politics along race and gender lines, which should have nothing to do with how you vote. What does matter — in Michigan as elsewhere — is that progressives like El-Sayed are pushing Medicare for All and want to eliminate the kind of gold-plated private insurance packages that unions like the UAW have worked so hard to win. El-Sayed claims that if you like your existing insurance, you can keep it, reminding us of President Obama’s false promise that "If you like your healthcare plan, you can keep it." That canard was PolitiFact’s Lie of the Year in 2013 after Obamacare caused millions of plans to be canceled. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION What matters in New York and many other Democratic-led states is that taxes will have to go up to cover the promises made by far-left politicians. You cannot provide free healthcare, free childcare and free services to people in the U.S. illegally without boosting taxes. New York is already the most-taxed state in the country. The budget for the state is twice that of Florida despite having fewer residents; this is unsustainable. What matters across the country is maintaining U.S. energy self-sufficiency and boosting employment. When New York progressive Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez calls to shut down fossil fuel production and Gov. Kathy Hochul slaps a moratorium on new hyperscale data centers, they are embracing policies that will cost their state jobs and incomes. That matters. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP President Trump was elected on a common-sense, pro-growth agenda. The Iran war complicates that message, but voters should remember that Democrats largely oppose the U.S.-led technological innovations that are driving progress worldwide, will block exploitation of America’s abundant fossil fuels, and will again embrace Joe Biden’s open border. articles.title: Amid 2028 speculation, Wes Moore urges Marylanders to back him on redistricting
articles.summary: Maryland’s Democratic governor is fighting a tough campaign in his state — and it’s not his re-election effort.
articles.body: BALTIMORE — Maryland Gov. Wes Moore is expected to cruise to re-election on Nov. 3. But he’s sweating the campaign nonetheless. Moore’s political prowess is being tested at home beyond his own race for a second term, as Maryland voters prepare to take sides on a ballot question that would allow state Democratic leaders to redraw congressional district lines in a way that favors the party even more than the current 7-1 map. Moore and his allies — including former President Barack Obama — are framing a vote for the ballot question as a vote to fight back against President Donald Trump and Republicans, an argument that might usually be expected to find purchase in a deep-blue state. But it has become apparent in recent weeks that support for the ballot measure may not be as strong as Moore and other Maryland Democrats had hoped, and a major late effort has ramped up to promote passage of the measure. If it doesn’t pass, it would be a major political setback for Moore amid wide speculation that he’s gearing up for a potential 2028 presidential campaign. Moore and his allies in Annapolis sought to redraw congressional districts this year, arguing that the Legislature could draw a map with all eight districts favoring Democrats to replace the current map in the wake of GOP redistricting efforts elsewhere. But the effort was halted by state Senate President Bill Ferguson, a fellow Democrat who claimed that the push didn’t have the support of a majority of lawmakers in his chamber. Ferguson noted that Maryland Democrats tried to draw a more favorable congressional district map in 2021, only for a state judge to toss it out in 2022. The ballot measure stemmed from that, seeking to address the state constitutional issue that sank the 2021 map first. In August, Ferguson and other Democrats in the Legislature overwhelmingly moved to put a measure before voters to eliminate the requirement that Maryland’s congressional districts obey natural boundaries, like the Chesapeake Bay. The state’s lone GOP U.S. House member, Andy Harris, represents a district concentrated on the state’s Eastern Shore. After a legal challenge, Maryland’s Supreme Court allowed the question to be put to voters in a form rewritten by state judges. With Election Day closing in, passage of the ballot question is far from certain. A poll released this month by the University of Maryland, Baltimore County, found that a majority of likely Maryland voters (53%) planned to vote against the measure. That included 42% of Democrats, 74% of Republicans and 59% of unaffiliated voters who planned to vote no. “To me, there was a broader underlying, interesting question about democracy. Do people want district lines to favor one party over the other? And most Marylanders don’t like that idea,” Mileah Kromer, the director of the UMBC Institute of Politics, told NBC News. Kromer’s survey used plain language instead of the legalese that will appear on the ballot defining Question 3 and still found broad opposition from members of both parties and independent voters. “Certainly there are a lot of Democrats who want to see some fighting back against President Trump but maybe don’t believe that, you know, redrawing congressional district lines just to favor their outcome is the way that they’d like to do it,” Kromer said. She added that part of the reluctance of Maryland voters in particular is the fact that Democrats would gain only one seat in redistricting efforts. A similar measure that passed in California last year allowed the state to redraw congressional district lines in a way that gained Democrats advantages in five seats, overriding the state’s independent redistricting commission just months after Texas redrew its congressional maps to boost Republicans in an additional five seats. A national fight over district lines The two states’ moves last year set off yet more state redistricting efforts this year. A number of red states succeeded in redrawing their maps, while others still face legal challenges. A longtime Democratic strategist in Maryland also pointed to the fact that Maryland voters are usually especially well-informed about national politics, particularly those who live in counties that border Washington. “I wonder if there aren’t a lot of people in the state, Democrats in particular, who don’t feel like co-opting the Republican strategy of mid-decade redistricting is the best way to fight back,” said the strategist, who, like others in this article, was granted anonymity to speak candidly. “If they heard anything in the news about mid-decade redistricting, it’s about, you know, Republicans or Donald Trump breaking the rules. They may not be that comfortable with that.” Still, Kromer cautioned that the UMBC survey was conducted before the groups backing and opposing the ballot question began spending heavily on TV, digital and physical advertising. Maryland’s Democratic voters are “upset about the Trump administration, and the messaging of, like, fighting back against Trump could be a really, really good messaging strategy,” Kromer said. “It might actually knock people more into the attitude of ‘I don’t like it, but it’s necessary.’” After the poll was released last month, Moore and his allies began spending in earnest to persuade voters to support the ballot measure. So far this month, Fight Back MD, a group supporting the measure, has spent $550,000 on TV ads urging voters to vote in favor of Question 3, according to AdImpact. Last week, Moore’s campaign decided to switch advertising from promoting his re-election bid to urging voters to support the measure. But even raising money among Democrats to support the measure has been an uphill battle, with the redistricting divide between Moore and Ferguson still present behind the scenes. Moore’s campaign released an ad last week featuring some of the state’s Democratic leaders urging voters to support Question 3, which was backed by a $700,000 investment by the campaign. On Monday, the campaign used an additional $500,000 on a TV and digital ad featuring Obama telling voters to support Question 3. One state leader noticeably absent from the push is Ferguson. While he worked in August to convene a special session to pass a measure to put the redistricting question to voters, he hasn’t publicly or privately committed to pursue redistricting during next year’s legislative session if it passes next month. Meanwhile, some donors who had expressed interest in the redistricting campaign have shown hesitation to donate this fall because Ferguson refuses to commit to passing new congressional maps, according to an operative familiar with the pro-Question 3 campaign. Ferguson’s communications director, David Schuhlein, told NBC News that Ferguson “is primarily focused on retaining our Democratic state Senate seats and also trying to build on that and gain one or two more in a couple of districts throughout the state, and that takes an immense effort from him and the rest of our leadership team.” “That’s where most of his efforts have been focused from the primary till now,” Schuhlein added. Redistricting on the 2028 campaign trail Moore in recent years has demurred about his potential presidential aspirations, but his out-of-state travel schedule has fueled speculation. Last year, he told NBC News’ “Meet the Press,” “Yeah, I’m not running for president,” adding that he was focused on his re-election bid. But in a gubernatorial debate this month against his GOP opponent, former state Del. Dan Cox, Moore didn’t commit to serve a full term if he’s re-elected this fall. “Being the governor of Maryland has been the honor of a lifetime,” he told debate moderators when he was asked whether he’d commit to serve a full second term. “And I would not be running for re-election if I was not committed to the people of Maryland.” Republicans in the state, who oppose Question 3, have accused Moore of pushing redistricting in Maryland to bolster his political aspirations. A digital video produced by the state’s conservative Freedom Caucus tells viewers that 100% Democratic control of Maryland’s eight congressional districts would be “a trophy for his run at the White House.” But some of Moore’s allies stressed that even if Moore fails to persuade voters to pass Question 3, it wouldn’t be a stain on a future presidential run. “I just cannot imagine people caring that much about this” outside Maryland, a national Democratic strategist told NBC News. “He has a great record to talk about on issues people care about. ‘You didn’t knock off Andy Harris’ is not going to be an issue in early [Democratic presidential primary] states.” “This is not the end-all, be-all for his political aspirations,” the strategist added. Michael Hanmer, the director of the Center for Democracy and Civic Engagement at the University of Maryland, told NBC News, “The average voter, they’re not going to notice and they’re not going to care in terms of how they think about this when they’re looking at the candidates.” “The problem in that situation, if it doesn’t pass, is that opponents are going to bring it up, and they’re going to use it as an example. They’re going to say: ‘Look at the makeup of your state. You couldn’t get this? It was just one; you couldn’t flip one?’” Hanmer added. He predicted that redistricting and how elected officials wield political power in their states could emerge as a wedge between potential 2028 candidates, particularly governors, because of their broad agreements on issues like the economy, foreign affairs and immigration. “I don’t think that we’re going to see a lot of candidates with massive distance between themselves on policy, right?” Hanmer said. He added: “Gov. Moore is an extremely skilled politician. He is extremely, I think, quick on his feet and smart. I am sure he will have a response, but I would be surprised if [redistricting] is not something that others — if they were successful and he was not — bring up.”

articles.title: Obama cozies up to Dem Party's socialist wing as former president makes surprising midterm moves
articles.summary: Barack Obama rallied for Abdul El-Sayed in Detroit and endorsed progressive Democrats who back Medicare for All and higher taxes on billionaires.
articles.body: Former President Barack Obama is increasingly throwing his political weight behind socialist and socialist-aligned Democrats as the party's left wing gains ground ahead of the midterm elections. Democratic Socialists of America-backed candidates have scored several notable primary victories this year, adding to signs of the left wing's growing influence in Democratic politics ahead of November's midterms. While Obama is not backing every socialist candidate, his recent endorsements and campaign appearances show he is willing to bring some of the party’s most progressive figures into the Democratic coalition. "President Obama remains the most popular figure in Democratic politics and a kingmaker whose support candidates actively seek," Democratic strategist Kevin Walling told Fox News Digital of the president who left office nearly a decade ago. "He understands that a Democrat who can win in New York City and a Democrat who can win in Michigan and Ohio have different politics, and the ability to bring those people into the same coalition is exactly what makes him so valuable." BIDEN CONSPICUOUSLY ABSENT FROM CAMPAIGN TRAIL AS OBAMA, HARRIS STEP UP FOR MIDTERM PUSH Obama's embrace of the party's progressive wing was on display Saturday in Michigan, where he campaigned alongside Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, while also lending his support to Florida Senate nominee Angie Nixon in a campaign video. While El-Sayed does not identify as a democratic socialist or a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, he has embraced progressive policies, including Medicare for All, that have become central to the party's left wing. During the Michigan rally, Obama invoked healthcare to defend Democrats against accusations that the party has moved too far to the left. "What is so radical about wanting everybody to have health care?" Obama asked, as he promoted El-Sayed’s pledge to expand access to affordable coverage. Obama’s comments prompted critics to revisit his own Obamacare-era promises and question the affordability of health care under his signature law. One X commenter sarcastically asked, "I thought someone fixed health care. What happened?" Another responded, "Who’s going to tell him?" Obama praised Nixon for championing a $15 minimum wage and opposing Republican-backed congressional redistricting maps, calling her a leader "willing to stand up again and again for what’s right" who would make "an outstanding U.S. Senator." Nixon, a DSA member, is campaigning on Medicare for All, universal childcare, rent protections and higher taxes on billionaires. The former president has also campaigned with Texas Senate candidate James Talarico, whom Republicans have branded a democratic socialist. Talarico has emphasized economic populism, universal health care, stronger unions and campaign-finance restrictions, but does not identify as a socialist. OBAMA'S STAR POWER GETS A REALITY CHECK FROM BLACK VOTERS IN CRUCIAL SENATE RACE: 'IT'S A TURNOFF' Obama’s outreach comes amid a series of primary victories by democratic socialists and other left-wing challengers this year. In Colorado, Melat Kiros defeated longtime Democratic Rep. Diana DeGette, while Donavan McKinney ousted Rep. Shri Thanedar in Michigan. Socialist-backed candidates also won congressional primaries in New York, building on Zohran Mamdani’s 2025 mayoral victory. Obama's support for the party's socialist left is not new. The former president endorsed Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez in her 2018 congressional race and former Rep. Jamaal Bowman in 2020, both of whom received backing from the Democratic Socialists of America. Obama’s public praise of figures tied to communist movements also extends beyond his current campaign allies. He has repeatedly celebrated Nelson Mandela, who had documented ties to South Africa’s Communist Party, and wrote warmly in "Dreams from My Father" about Frank Marshall Davis, a former Communist Party USA figure who served as a mentor during Obama’s youth. Obama also reached out to Mamdani during his 2025 campaign for New York City mayor, praising the democratic socialist's campaign and offering to serve as a sounding board without formally endorsing his candidacy. DSA’S GROWING GRIP ON DEM PARTY HITS NEW TERRITORY AS ESTABLISHMENT FALLS IN LINE Democratic strategist Mally Smith defended Obama’s campaign activity, arguing that his support reflects an effort to build a broad coalition rather than a wholesale endorsement of every progressive policy. "President Obama is, by far, the most popular politician in America. He is traveling around the country supporting Democrats from across the party," Smith told Fox News Digital. "He understands we need a big-tent coalition, and that is why he is helping Democrats as diverse as Josh Turek in Iowa to El-Sayed in Michigan." "The Republicans have no equivalent when it comes to Obama’s broad appeal across the electorate," Smith said. "They are stuck with Trump, who is on a red-state desperation tour because he can’t step foot in any swing state since at-risk Republicans don’t want to be anywhere near him." At a campaign rally in Kansas, President Trump called Obama "a rotten president," while dismissing his planned appearance with El-Sayed. "I love Michigan. I don’t believe that Michigan values are gonna allow this guy to get in. He’s an arrogant guy. But Barack Hussein Obama is going up there to help him campaign," said Trump. WHO IS ANGIE NIXON? BULLHORN-WIELDING SOCIALIST UPSETS ESTABLISHMENT FAVORITE IN SUNSHINE STATE STUNNER Walling said Obama’s strength comes from his ability to support candidates with different political profiles while keeping them under the same Democratic umbrella. "The former president doesn’t ask which wing of the party a nominee comes from. He asks whether they can win, and he’s helping Democrats build a party broad enough to compete to do just that," Walling said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Obama’s return to the campaign trail comes as Democrats debate whether the party can turn the energy of its socialist and progressive movements into a national coalition — and whether candidates backed by the party’s left can win beyond deep-blue cities and districts. Fox News Digital reached out to Obama's office for comment but did not immediately receive a reply.

articles.title: Senate braces for nasty fight over seating Peltola after Alaska Senate race
articles.summary: Senators are bracing for a potential floor fight over accepting the results of the Alaska Senate race between incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) and former Rep. Mary Peltola (D) — and perhaps other battleground contests — if President Trump urges allies to dispute what he might view as unfair or “rigged” results. Democratic senators generally…
articles.body:
Senators are bracing for a potential floor fight over accepting the results of the Alaska Senate race between incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) and former Rep. Mary Peltola (D) — and perhaps other battleground contests — if President Trump urges allies to dispute what he might view as unfair or “rigged” results.

Democratic senators generally view Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) as a straight shooter who would be averse to rejecting an election result in an Alaska Senate race certified by the governor and lieutenant governor.

But they aren’t ruling out the possibility that the president will prod his MAGA allies in the Senate to contest the election results if Sen. Dan Sullivan loses by a narrow margin and blames his loss on voter confusion leading to a significant number of votes for his opponent with a similar name, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.

If Alaska’s top officials certify Peltola as the winner, and Trump calls on Senate allies to reject that finding, it puts Thune in a tough spot and potentially sets up a messy floor fight.

“Everybody is gaming everything out, and everybody is preparing for everything,” a Senate Democratic aide said of the preparations for potential Republican objections if Peltola narrowly beats the incumbent Republican senator.

Sarah Binder, a professor of political science at George Washington University and a Senate rules expert, said Trump’s aggressive threat to challenge a Democratic win in Alaska could lead to a nasty Senate floor fight.

“We can’t rule anything out at this stage just given the president’s single-minded persistence that there’s a lot of electoral fraud conducted by Democrats,” she said.

“Would he push Republicans to object to the seating, if Alaska certified the seating of Peltola? The second question is, if he did that, would Republicans actually follow through?” Binder continued.

“That gets us into the hornet’s nest of what the Senate would do to challenge a literal swearing in,” she added. “There’s no single charted pathway here.”

She noted that, historically, if Alaska certifies Peltola as the winner over Sen. Dan Sullivan, Republicans could object to swearing her in.

“I could imagine a scenario where they would want to swear her in, and somebody objects,” she said.

Senate sources familiar with how the floor process would play out said that a Trump-allied senator or a group of GOP senators could signal an intention to object to Peltola — or to the Democratic winner of another close Senate race where Trump might claim election fraud — taking the oath of office to become senator in 2027.

That would then lead to a negotiation between Thune and Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) over how to resolve the situation.

Senate Republican sources say they’re confident that incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan will defeat Peltola next week.

Recent polls show Peltola leading the GOP senator by 2 percentage points, but the race is within the margin of error.

Recent surveys by Data for Progress, InsiderAdvantage and Alaska Survey Research showed the Democrat leading by 2 points while a New York Times/Siena poll conducted from Sept. 24 to Oct. 1 showed her ahead of Sullivan by 7 points.

Alaska has ranked-choice voting, which could shift how some votes are counted.

One relevant Senate precedent comes from January 1997, when Republican candidate Woody Jenkins petitioned the Senate to throw out Democrat Mary Landrieu’s victory in the 1996 Senate race in Louisiana.

Landrieu won by more than 5,000 votes, but Jenkins alleged “widespread vote tampering.”

Senate leaders resolved the matter by agreeing to seat Landrieu “without prejudice” and referring the allegations of election fraud to the Senate Rules Committee to investigate. The deal left open the door to the Senate voting to unseat Landrieu by a majority vote if the charges of cheating were substantiated.

In the end, the Rules Committee voted unanimously in October 1997 to end its investigation and clear Landrieu of wrongdoing even though it acknowledged some voting irregularities.

Trump is laying the groundwork for a similar fight this fall if Peltola wins, giving Democrats a crucial pickup in a GOP-leaning state.

The Trump Justice Department last week asked a federal court to block the certification of the winner of the Alaska Senate race if Sen. Dan Sullivan loses by a narrow margin and could argue that he would have won if his near-namesake, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., hadn’t been on the ballot.

Legal experts have broadly dismissed the Justice Department lawsuit as meritless, raising the prospect that Trump’s next move may be to demand that GOP senators refuse to seat Peltola if she wins by a small margin.

“They’ve set up the argument already that there’s a deliberate deception on the part of the other Dan Sullivan, and even though this seems to have been adjudicated in Alaska law, they will certainly argue the issue of fairness remains,” said Steven S. Smith, a professor of political science at Arizona State University, who follows Senate politics.

Alaska’s Division of Elections, which is led by the state’s Republican lieutenant governor, initially removed “Dan J. Sullivan” from the ballot, but a state judge later ruled that he be placed back on the ballot.

The Alaska Supreme Court upheld that decision .

To avoid confusion, the Alaska ballot lists “Dan S. Sullivan” as the Republican incumbent and lists his opponent as “Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.” without party affiliation.

Given that the Alaska Supreme Court has already ruled that the little-known Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. deserves a spot on the ballot, it would be hard to see how state officials could withhold the certification of a narrow Peltola victory without being overturned by the courts, legal experts say.

That then sets the stage for a fight in the Senate, where any number of Trump allies or ambitious Republican senators who are looking for a springboard for national publicity could object to seating Peltola.

“This is really a question of Trump-backed Republicans, and I think with Trump probably urging them to exploit every opening, the certification of the Democrat will lead to a Republican challenge if they’re in a position in the Senate to do so,” Smith said.

If Peltola wins her race by a narrow margin, however, she will need Alaska’s Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy and Lt. Gov. Nancy Dahlstrom, who handles the duties of the secretary of State, to certify her victory.

If Republican state officials refuse to certify a Peltola victory, then Senate Republicans argue the Senate rules would not allow the upper chamber to seat her when the Senate convenes for the new Congress on Jan. 3.

The matter would need to be resolved by Alaska’s courts.

A similar stalemate played out in 2009 after the close contest between Democrat Al Franken and GOP Sen. Norm Coleman in Minnesota.

The state’s Republican Gov. Tim Pawlenty signed the election certificate validating Franken’s victory only after the Minnesota Supreme Court unanimously ruled in June 2009 that Franken had won the race by just more than 200 votes.

Democrats, who had 59 seats at the time, agreed not to seat Franken until the legal process played out.

articles.title: Another change election and a whipsawed America
articles.summary: The most likely scenario for next week’s election is … that no one will learn anything. articles.body:
The most likely scenario for next week’s election is … that no one will learn anything.

I can say that with some degree of confidence because in the last five election cycles or so, the learning curve has been so flat that if it was a politician’s posterior, President Trump wouldn’t even notice it.

Campaigns, individuals, parties and super PACs are going to have spent northward of $12 billion on this year’s midterms. That will end up being something like $115 for every voter, but all they’ll have to show for it is a kitchen trashcan full of junk mail. Washington has been a ghost town for weeks as lawmakers dare not be caught making any laws so close to the election. News outlets from the most local to the international have shifted into constant coverage mode for what is, even in the most robust case, a relatively low-turnout, low-stakes election.

We are — by virtue of both the curse that has afflicted the party in power in all but three midterm elections since the Civil War and sky-high consumer prices — heading for divided government. Gridlock is coming. How big the Democratic majority is in the House or whether the blue team can manage a clean sweep in Senate races to take the upper chamber isn’t a matter of no importance, but it is certainly an issue of marginal significance.

It matters a great deal to me because I have, as imprudent and self-flagellatory as it may seem to you, devoted my vocational life to the questions with answers hidden deep within the crosstabs of exit polls, swing district turnout numbers and in the arcana of Senate procedure. I care about those things because I want to know where the country is going, but also because I’m interested in where we’ve been.

Next week’s results will still tell me something about what’s happening under the hood in the engine of this beautiful big-block V8 of a nation. Alas, though, I already know what I’ll likely find: People are frustrated, fed up and want something else.

American voters have been seeking one thing above all others since at least 2014: change. In that time, we’ve seen control of the House flip three times and the Senate change hands twice, plus one 50-50 tie. We are heading for a fourth change in the House and maybe a third switch in the Senate in just 12 years. Not only is that more flipping than in the first part of this century, but the majorities have also been shorter in duration and smaller in size than in even that relatively choppy period.

Like a frustrated IT worker on the help desk, the American electorate keeps saying to the government: Have you tried turning it off and then turning it back on?

And just like the technophobic employee at the other end of the line, Washington only responds with an error message.

There have been at least three substantial political realignments in the past 100 years in which the parties have dramatically changed their geographic and demographic coalitions, but you’d still have to go all the way back to the 1870s and 1880s to find a period as politically unsettled as our own. That was the last time we saw such unstable majorities in Congress. And the last time the presidency switched parties in three consecutive elections was from 1884 to 1892. That was also, not coincidentally, the last time a president served nonconsecutive terms — the criminally underrated Grover Cleveland.

Our Gilded Age forebears even went for a fourth presidential flip, sending the White House back over the net in 1896. And if you were betting, you’d say that we were going to do the same in 2028.

The reasons for the instability today have some substantial overlap with the causes back in the days of girthsome Grover. Weak national parties have been supplanted by other forces: wealthy patrons and populistic mobs. William Jennings Bryan knew the Hasan Pikers of his day, and J.P. Morgan would have had to tip his cap to Elon Musk.

But also, the nation itself is unsettled. Like the post-Civil War era, America is going through a long period of demographic, technological, economic and social change. The nation faces the future with a mix of hopeful wonder and profound dread. Whether it’s electrification or artificial intelligence, big changes to the ways that people live and work are bound to be reflected in their political preferences.

Now, as it was then, we have declining birth rates, lots of immigration, shifting population centers and a sometimes-violent clash between tradition and progress. And in the most Gilded Age feature of all, rank corruption has convinced many that the system itself may be beyond saving.

If you’re a Democrat, you need to believe that the arc of history will start bending away from the entropy of the 2010s and 2020s on a bracing fall night a week from today. You have to believe that because, otherwise, what have you been annoying your friends and family for all these weeks?

The same goes for Republicans. You have to believe that a heroic goal line stands to save the Senate and keep the governorship of some state you don’t even live in really matters. If not, what was the point of all those Facebook comments?

But take it from me, we are nowhere near the end of the entropy. Next week won’t solve anything. It will only again express the electorate’s wish for something different. But, maddeningly, not what that something should be.

That’s the question we’ll start hashing out as soon as the last votes are cast next Tuesday and begin a presidential cycle under the glaring judgment of an electorate that only seems to agree that whatever it is we’ve been doing hasn’t been working. But just don’t count on any of the candidates to take that lesson from the results.

articles.title: Democrats poised to go big on affordable childcare
articles.summary: Heading into a potential new political era, Democratic candidates, policymakers and outside groups all agree on one thing: Something needs to be done on childcare. Should they win a majority in Congress in November, the Democratic affordability agenda includes childcare as one of many everyday costs Democrats want to bring down. Democrats up and…
articles.body:
Heading into a potential new political era, Democratic candidates, policymakers and outside groups all agree on one thing: Something needs to be done on childcare.

Should they win a majority in Congress in November, the Democratic affordability agenda includes childcare as one of many everyday costs Democrats want to bring down.

Democrats up and down the ballot have been buzzing about fixing childcare with renewed fervor in recent years.

Nearly every Democratic candidate running for the Senate has a childcare agenda, and the most significant Democratic victories of the off-year elections — the gubernatorial races in New Jersey and Virginia and the New York City mayoral race — leaned heavily on the candidates’ focuses on childcare subsidies and availability.

But there’s daylight between different camps on exactly the right way forward, and the issue is one of a number that leadership will have to shuffle through and prioritize if Democrats take control.

It could also create lanes for the 2028 Democratic presidential primary.

“I absolutely think it’s become a prerequisite for running for president that you need to have a plan to solve for childcare and make sure that families can have safe nurturing care that they need for their kids,” said Julie Kashen, founder and principal of Women’s Economic Futures, a new policy and research initiative focused on childcare.

There’s little doubt that the energy to get something done about childcare is at a high-water point. During the COVID-19 pandemic, Congress allocated billions in emergency supplemental funding to help states manage the childcare sector, but most of those funds expired in 2024.

Kashen said those resources showed what could be if the federal government invested in childcare more permanently.

“The pandemic kind of pulled the invisibility cloak off of this issue that had been there all along, and as a result of that, it became an even hotter topic,” Kashen said. “And then, when the pandemic relief funding went to every state, and states actually innovated with public funding, people really saw what was possible, and that it could really make a difference to making childcare more affordable, more stable.”

Democratic lawmakers in the last year or so have started staking out their wishlists on specific childcare policies. Sens. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) and Patty Murray (D-Wash.) are the Senate co-chairs of a childcare working group, along with Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) and Bobby Scott (D-Va.) in the House.

Warren and Murray, backed by the caucus, released a framework for childcare affordability in June. Although light on specifics, that framework mentions “building a strong and stable public infrastructure” for childcare and increasing pay and benefits for childcare workers.

“Democrats understand that childcare is fundamental economic infrastructure and an important way we can deliver to lower costs for the American people—affordable and accessible high-quality childcare is a priority for families so childcare will absolutely be a priority for members in the next Congress,” a Senate Democratic aide told The Hill.

Rep. Katherine Clark (Mass.), the Democratic whip whose role will become even more powerful if Democrats win the House majority, has pushed for expansive childcare legislation, including her Child Care is Infrastructure Act , a package of two bills that help communities build more childcare facilities and repay student loans for early childhood educators.

Rep. Suzanne Bonamici (D-Ore.), who is challenging Scott for the top Democratic post on the House Education and Workforce Committee, has also led efforts to support the Head Start educator workforce, among other childcare proposals. So have Rep. Sara Jacobs (D-Calif.) and many others .

Several states and localities have picked up on the momentum in recent years: New York City has begun to roll out universal free childcare programs for 3- and 4-year-olds. Washington, D.C., offers free pre-K for 3- and 4-year-olds in public schools. New Mexico passed a law earlier this year that guarantees no-cost childcare to residents, balanced out by the state’s oil revenues.

Now, advocates are hoping Congress seizes the opportunity to pass a more substantive childcare package that supports both the workforce and the families who need care.

“I do think that any solution must have a supply side answer to it … like you can’t just put money into tax credits and hope for the best,” Kashen said. “We do not have enough childcare for every family that wants it, and even when we do have it, a lot of families can’t afford it. So we need to make sure that we’re investing in making sure there’s good quality childcare, that there’s childcare that works for every family that’s available, so it can’t just be a solution that gives parents more money because they won’t have anywhere to use that money.”

Affordable childcare isn’t a solely Democratic issue: In 1971, Congress passed a bipartisan bill that would have established a national daycare system funded by billions in federal dollars.

Some Republicans in Congress have picked up the torch to push for legislative childcare reforms, including reauthorizing the Child Care and Development Block Grant program, which gives states federal funding to help low-income families get childcare.

Yet President Trump has looked to federal childcare programs as opportunities to dial down federal spending and regulation and eliminate fraud.

The administration wants to roll back regulations on Head Start, a federal childcare program for low-income children. The administration proposed a rule earlier this year that would turn the responsibility of setting Head Start regulations for class sizes, background checks and other requirements over to the states. Administration officials argue the changes would loosen unnecessary federal spending and oversight while opening up more seats in the states.

Democrats and advocates want to be ambitious.

That could mean some form of federal universal childcare, although the term is somewhat nebulous. Some Democratic candidates — including Angie Nixon in Florida, James Talarico in Texas and Troy Jackson in Maine — have backed universal childcare in their campaign platforms.

Democratic strategists, meanwhile, put together Project 2029, an agenda charting a specific policy course for a future Democratic administration on a range of issues.

That framework is twofold : It suggests a free childcare option consisting of publicly funded childcare slots in a range of trusted settings for everyone regardless of income, including Head Start, faith-based providers, public schools, home-based care and other options. Additionally, the framework suggests another option called CareCredit, a financial stipend of $1,000 a month to any family that chooses not to use one of their free slots, administered federally.

Tara McGuinness, executive director of the New Practice Lab at New America, a liberal think tank, helped write the childcare section. She said their vision could pick up bipartisan support because of how much flexibility it gives parents.

“If you listen to parents, we need more than one thing,” McGuinness said. “We don’t have access to paid family medical leave, and many parents, moms and dads, want to have time in those very early years with their own kids. The cash credit could help tackle that, and we do not have enough access to affordable, quality childcare, and we need more public investment in order to do that.”

Daniel Hains, chief policy officer at the National Association for the Education of Young Children, said the political momentum for ambitious legislation on childcare and more examples of state programs as models could be the right conditions to pass a childcare equivalent of the Affordable Care Act. He compared the current state of play with the decades of healthcare reform that came before that bill.

“I think with all of the continued momentum, continued storytelling, I think we’re in a similar place where we have, you know, we did not succeed, in the pandemic, passing the long term transformational investments,” Hains said. “We passed the investments that were needed to keep the sector afloat, and I think there’s still a need for the transformational investments, and policymakers understand that.”

articles.title: Inside Trump’s red state blitz to stave off a Democratic midterm sweep
articles.summary: Republicans are working to salvage the House and Senate maps one week before Election Day as the chance of a Democratic sweep becomes more likely. articles.body:
Republicans are working to salvage the House and Senate maps one week before Election Day as the chance of a Democratic sweep becomes more likely.

Turnout has played a central role in the GOP’s strategy despite midterm election cycles often yielding lower turnout than presidential years. The party has argued that President Trump’s presence on the trail coupled with his calls for supporters to “pretend” he is on the ballot will help Republicans replicate the coalition that propelled Trump to victory in 2023.

But discontent with Trump’s handling of the economy paired with the fallout over the Iran war is threatening to dampen Republican enthusiasm and persuade swing voters, putting Democrats on a potential glide path to victory.

While Trump has visited a number of swing states and is on track to visit more before Election Day, he has made several campaign stops in traditionally red strongholds. In the lead-up to Nov. 3, Trump has rallied in Kentucky , Alabama , Nebraska , Mississippi , Oklahoma and Tennessee . He won all these states by double digits in 2024.

“This looks both necessary and risky,” one Republican strategist said of Trump’s red-state blitz. “We’re playing defense in some red states here. It’s not a notion of persuading or winning back independents or some that broke our way in ‘24. It’s about ensuring that every MAGA vote possible comes out.”

Kentucky is home to the highly competitive race to replace Rep. Andy Barr (R) in the 6th District. Trump’s October stop in the Bluegrass State’s 4th District also took place in the Cincinnati media market, which allowed him to message in battleground Ohio as well.

In Alabama, Republicans see the state’s 2nd District as a prime pickup opportunity after redistricting. And in Nebraska, Sen. Pete Ricketts (R) is facing a more competitive race in part due to the war in Iran’s impact on agriculture-dominant states.

But one of the most eyebrow-raising red state visits from Trump came just eight days out from Election Day in Mississippi, where Trump campaigned for Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in Corinth following a number of stops in the state from high-profile Democrats.

Veteran Republican strategist Rob Stutzman called the midterm strategy of deploying the sitting president to red states as “conventional.”

“You’re going to South Carolina, Florida and Mississippi this week,” Stutzman said. “That’s a strategy to make sure the bottom doesn’t fall out.”

Trump has chalked up his visits to the GOP strongholds as a way to “pay respect to his supporters.”

Vice President Vance has also traveled to red-leaning and toss-up states. On Monday, the vice president rallied Republicans in Belgrade, Mont. — which is home to the state’s toss-up 1st District — as well as Topeka, Kan., where Republican Sen. Roger Marshall is locked in a tougher-than-expected reelection bid.

The unnamed Republican strategist likened the trips to red bastions, in particular, as “a farewell tour,” warning that visits to battleground states could do more damage than good.

“Dems have been playing in our sandbox, why don’t we stick the president in places where he can do no damage or maybe minimal damage?” the strategist continued.

According to a Monday polling average from Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), Trump’s approval sits at 39.3 percent while his disapproval is at 59.3 percent. Republicans on the generic congressional ballot do not appear to be fairing any better. Democrats lead 51 percent to 43.1 percent, per DDHQ.

Still, a number of incumbents and candidates in tough contests have appeared with Trump and Vance in the final stretch. Michigan Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers joined Trump at a rally in Port Huron, Mich., over the weekend, while Iowa Republican Senate nominee Ashley Hinson campaigned with Trump in Sioux City, Iowa, on Thursday.

A few vulnerable House Republicans in both states — Reps. Tom Barrett (Mich.), Mariannette Miller-Meeks (Iowa) and Zach Nunn (Iowa) — were absent from the events. The three lawmakers previously appeared publicly with Trump this cycle.

“At the end of the day, the Democrats are going to label our candidates as MAGA, Trump, whatever label they want to slap on us, and we accept that fact,” a national Republican operative told The Hill.

“We encourage more Trump engagement,” the operative continued, noting that Trump is “very, very key” to making the Republican base turnout.

Trump’s political operation, MAGA Inc., has also played a major role in supporting Republican candidates this midterm cycle. Last week, the president said he and his political operation will spend more than $400 million to back Republican candidates. According to recent Federal Election Commission filings, the president’s MAGA Inc. super PAC has spent $277 million over the last six weeks.

Other outside entities backing Republicans have injected cash into the midterms as well, including Americans for Prosperity and tech giant Elon Musk, who has poured more than $400 million into races this cycle.

On top of that, the Republican National Committee (RNC) announced last week it moved over $44 million to the National Republican Congressional Committee and the National Republican Senatorial Committee from mid-August to mid-October. The two committees evenly split the funds and are both expected to receive $6 million more from the RNC before Election Day.

“This is the first time we’ve ever had two major super PAC at CLF [Congressional Leadership Fund] and MAGA Inc. fully involved in the House, so we’ll take all of the help we can get,” said the national operative.

However, Trump’s critics within his own party warn that his messaging on the campaign trail could backfire on Republicans.

The president made headlines over the weekend when he issued a 1,300-word Truth Social post slamming television host and comedian Bill Maher. Critics were quick to brand the post as unhinged.

“When things are going well economically, nobody really cares about some of the more crazy rhetoric, but when things are not going well, that’s where it becomes all the more problematic and preposterous,” the Republican strategist said.

Trump also raised eyebrows in a viral moment when he touted the profits the U.S. oil and gas industry has made from the war in Iran, adding that his advisers warned him not to talk about the topic.

The president did note in the same comments that oil prices would be “falling dramatically in a short period of time,” but some Republicans say the comment was out of touch with Americans grappling with high energy prices.

“Voters don’t want to hear that someone is getting rich in the abstract,” Stutzman said. “For all those that want to credit Trump with having his finger on the pulse of the common man, I think we’re all waiting to see that touch this week because it hasn’t been showing up.”
