articles.title: 'Dark money’ group accused of 'scheme' to tip election in favor of Democrats, manipulate GOP voters
articles.summary: American Forge Coalition mailers accuse vulnerable Republicans of supporting mass amnesty in key battleground districts ahead of the midterm election.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: A mysterious new group purporting to be part of an "anti-globalist," pro-American movement is targeting Republicans in battleground House races across the country in what some are calling a coordinated scheme to suppress GOP votes. The American Forge Coalition has sent out a flurry of mailers to voters this month accusing vulnerable Republicans of not being conservative enough. Some believe it's a coordinated effort by the left to depress GOP voter turnout in the midterm election just a week away. "This is a shady Democrat dark money scheme using a front group that isn't even registered with the [Federal Election Commission], mailing Republicans at the start of early voting to suppress them from turning out," Rep. Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., campaign spokesman Ciro Riccardi told Fox News Digital. In fact, an investigation by Fox News Digital found that the group's targets include Lawler's race in New York's 17th Congressional District, Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa., in Pennsylvania's 1st Congressional District, Rep. Derrick Van Orden, R-Wis., in Wisconsin's 3rd Congressional District, Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, R-Iowa, in Iowa's 1st Congressional District, Rep. Jen Kiggans, R-Va., in Virginia's 2nd Congressional District, and Laurie Buckhout, who is running to unseat Rep. Don Davis, D-N.C., in North Carolina's 1st Congressional District. TOP ELECTION SCHEMES ROILING KEY MIDTERM RACES AS BOTH PARTIES ACCUSE RIVALS OF TRICKERY In Lawler's, Kiggans' and Fitzpatrick's cases, the group sent mailers accusing them of supporting "mass amnesty" and "letting criminals escape justice after illegally entering our nation." Mailers sent in Van Orden and Buckhout's races accused them of being too lenient on abortion. Mailers sent in North Carolina claimed Buckhout supports "abortions up until birth," while Wisconsin voters got flyers that said Van Orden "would allow the murder of the unborn into the second trimester." Both attack lines take liberties with the truth. Lawler, Fitzpatrick and Kiggans all support the Dignity Act, which establishes a pathway to temporary legal status for undocumented migrants provided they pay certain fees and pass a background check, while also increasing pay for Border Patrol. But none support amnesty for illegal immigrants with criminal histories. In the case of Van Orden and Buckhout, both have positioned themselves as pro-life and have been attacked by Democrats as "anti-abortion." 'NO KINGS' FOOT SOLDIERS IGNORE ORGANIZERS' WARNING, GO ALL IN FOR DEMOCRATS "They are obviously a left-wing dark money group. This is unfortunately not a new tactic by them. And they are really hurting our country," Fitzpatrick's campaign told Fox News Digital. "They are telling Republicans that we are too independent, and then telling Democrats that we're not independent enough." Buckhout's campaign accused the group of "lying to eastern North Carolina voters," adding, "Their fake ads are designed to split the Republican vote." It is not clear where the American Forge Coalition's money or support is coming from, and it almost appears deliberately structured to obscure that information. WHAT STRANGERS CAN LEARN FROM YOUR POLITICAL DONATION The group is registered as a 501(c)(4) social welfare organization or advocacy group rather than a political action committee (PAC), meaning it does not need to disclose its financial information with the FEC. Groups registered as 501(c)(4) are permitted to advocate for certain issues but barred by law from directly campaigning for a specific candidate in an election. "There are liberal and conservative groups that have been taking advantage of the Supreme Court Citizens United ruling to spend secret money in our elections," Money in Politics Reform Director Michael Beckel told Fox News Digital. "When you've got a group like the American Forge Coalition popping up, there is a very slim paper trail that somebody can follow to try to make heads or tails of how they are trying to exert influence in election, what special interests or wealthy mega-donors might truly be calling the shots for a group like this." Fitzpatrick's campaign said the goal of such groups "is to have a Congress where no more pragmatic, reasonable lawmakers are left." Caitlin Sutherland, executive director at Americans for Public Trust, told Fox News Digital, "The funders behind this group are assuredly leaning left. So at the same time that they're highlighting threats to democracy, they're actively trying to suppress voters. That does seem to be incredibly hypocritical." Records show the group was created in May 2026 and registered in Delaware, a popular tax haven state. The Wilmington address it's registered at was highlighted in a 2012 New York Times story because it also happens to be the address of some 285,000 different businesses, from small companies to corporate giants like American Airlines, Google, and JPMorgan Chase. DNC LAWSUIT ACCUSES TRUMP ADMINISTRATION OF DIVERTING $20M IN FEDERAL FUNDS FOR 'PROPAGANDA' ADS "A lot of organizations on both the left and the right incorporate in Delaware, where the incorporation laws are generally viewed as pretty friendly. So from the business records alone, we know very little about the American Forge Coalition," Beckel said. He said it's very possible the group is being bankrolled by left-wing actors: "This could well be a group masquerading as a conservative entity that is bankrolled by liberal or Democratic-aligned donors, and the public really doesn't have enough to go on to be able to truly assess who the donors are behind these types of really outrageous attack ads." And there is precedent for such moves on both sides. In 2024, a California-based group linked to former Rep. Eric Swalwell, D-Calif., called "True Patriots PA" was accused of trying to sway voters away from Fitzpatrick in Pennsylvania toward his more right-wing primary challenger, in what appeared to be a bid to give Democrats an easier time in the general election. But Sutherland said American Forge Coalition's campaign stood out against past tactics in that it was not aimed at bolstering other candidates — just kneecapping Republicans. "We've seen it before where these liberal dark money groups pop up late in the cycle, and they try to act as a spoiler," she said. "I will say what seems unique about this situation is that they're not trying to promote a third-party candidate, but it really seems the intention is to get Republicans to stay at home. That to me does seem to be a departure this cycle." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Power Rankings project Democrats winning the House majority by 219 seats, compared to 198 seats likely for Republicans, with 18 remaining as toss-ups. Three of the races — Lawler's, Kiggans', and Miller-Meeks' — are projected to be Democratic pickups, while the remainder are toss-ups, meaning the mailers could potentially help edge the majority away from the GOP if successful. The group's website does not list any donors or leadership, nor many details at all. The website appears to be an appeal to the populist right, led with the phrase: "WE THE PEOPLE built this country. NOT politicians. NOT foreigners. We're hammering it back into shape — one job, one neighborhood, one law at a time." Its platform advocates for tariffs on "cheap imports," against outsourcing jobs, for building a border wall and deporting "criminals," and stopping "Washington and the globalists from dictating to working families." American Forge Coalition did not respond to a list of questions sent by Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Trump supporters confront Iran, affordability concerns with a message for critics: 'Give him time'
articles.summary: Trump rally-goers in Perry, Georgia, defend the president as gas prices hit $3.66 per gallon amid the Iran war and growing affordability concerns.
articles.body: Trump supporters in Georgia are standing behind the president amid rising affordability concerns and higher gas prices stemming from the Iran war, with one voter calling him the "best president" in her lifetime. While Trump's approval rating teetered at 36% and his disapproval rating stood at 64%, praise for Trump was high in Perry, Georgia, Saturday as he campaigned alongside Republican gubernatorial candidate Rick Jackson, CEO of a healthcare staffing group; Rep. Mike Collins, R-Ga., who is vying to unseat Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga.; and candidates in House races across the state. The race for Ossoff's seat is highly contentious, as Republicans are seeking a pickup that would help them maintain control of the Senate. Ossoff won the seat in a January 2021 runoff election by 1.22% — less than 55,000 votes. Trump, meanwhile, won Georgia in 2024 by 2.2%. He told voters Saturday to act like "he's on the ballot" come Nov. 3. Rallygoer Gloria Barkman said she supports Trump because he delivers on his promises. "I know people are upset because things don't look good with the gas and everything like that, but give him time and they'll be seeing the difference," Barkman said. FORMER NFL ALL-PRO RUNNING BACK JOINS PRESIDENT TRUMP FOR GEORGIA MIDTERMS RALLY Barkman's comments come as gas prices in Georgia hover around $3.66 per gallon, compared with an average of $2.72 per gallon in February, before the start of the Iran war. Iranian attacks on commercial vessels and threats to restrict shipping through the Strait of Hormuz have destabilized global oil markets, sending prices higher worldwide. The Iran war has been a major point of contention during Trump's second term, with about 65% of Americans disapproving of Trump's actions in the conflict, according to Pew. However, rallygoer Jim Taylor, an Air Force veteran, said temporarily higher prices at the pump are a price worth paying to ensure Iran doesn't have a nuclear weapon. "I guess what I'm most proud of is what the president's done in Iran," Taylor told Fox News Digital. "I know he's got a lot of criticism for it, but being a military veteran and a strong supporter of the military itself, I'm very, very proud that he was at least willing to step up and do what had to be done — to take care of the bigger picture because gas prices really wouldn't matter if a nuclear weapon went off in our country," Taylor continued. Trump said during the rally that oil prices would come down soon and also touted an inflation rate of 1.7% over the last three months. However, the latest official annual CPI inflation rate was 3.7% in September, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. SEN DAVE MCCORMICK: TRUMP ACCOUNTS GIVE ALL AMERICANS A STAKE IN PROSPERITY Meanwhile, rallygoer TJ Barb applauded Trump for the creation of Trump Accounts, investment accounts established under Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill Act. "The investment in children — that's significant," Barb told Fox News Digital. "Financial intelligence. He's going to start giving that to our kids." Barkman said she is voting to protect the country. "I don't want us to lose our country because we stand for the United States, and I'm going full force for Trump in supporting him and the Republicans," Barkman said. Taylor described the elections as an "uphill battle" and said that although he wasn't as familiar with Collins before the campaign cycle, Trump's backing carries significant weight. "I would vote for anybody that Trump endorses," Taylor said. "I think Mike's a good candidate." Barb, who described himself as not very political, said he was also not as familiar with Collins before this midterm cycle but trusts Trump's endorsement. "He can't be bought," Barb told Fox News Digital. "So when he's backing these guys, we know, all right, well, he's already shown what he's done, so this is what we're going to do," Barb told Fox News Digital. "And so it's just cut and paste and let's get another guy up in there." But after seeing Collins on Saturday, Barb said he identified with the candidate beyond Trump's endorsement. "Hearing his story, Blue collar stuff," Barb told Fox News Digital. "He's gone through it, I think that's what helps him relate to other folks. He's straight southern Georgia right there, I'll tell you. He's a good old, good old boy." AFTER 47 YEARS OF CONFRONTING IRAN, DOES AMERICA HAVE A STRATEGY FOR ENDING THIS WAR? John Salvesen, the Republican nominee in Georgia's 5th Congressional District, a Democratic stronghold in Atlanta previously represented by civil rights icon John Lewis, said he is a big fan of Collins. "I think he's wonderful. I like him a lot because he's a lot like me, we're just working dudes," Salvesen told Fox News Digital. "He's a logger. I'm a handyman, and we just didn't like what we saw, so it prompted us to run." "I think Jon Ossoff is terrible," Salvesen continued. "And I'm not saying that because I'm Republican. I'm saying it because I studied him, and Mike Collins is a superior candidate to him if he can get the message out to the right people." SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER "I think once you know Mike Collins or Rick Jackson, with or without Trump's support, you can't help but go for these guys not because they're Republicans because they are awesome candidates," Salvesen continued. Meanwhile, Barkman said she has followed Collins during his time in the House of Representatives and praised his voting record. "I've always been impressed with him," Barkman told Fox News Digital. "He's very personable, friendly. He reaches out to the people, and we love him." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP A spokesperson for Collins said he is "proud" to have Trump in his corner and is "out every day earning the trust of Georgians." "Like President Trump, Georgians are backing Mike Collins because he delivered the Laken Riley Act to deport criminal illegals, cut taxes for hardworking families, and is the only candidate who can beat radical leftist Jon Ossoff. Ossoff hates President Trump more than he loves Georgia, and Mike Collins is the bipartisan workhorse who will work with anybody to make Georgia safer and more prosperous," Meyer Siegfried, a spokesperson for Collins, said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Obama tries to gaslight America about Abdul El-Sayed
articles.summary: With just over a week to go until the midterm elections, former President Obama joined the campaign trail to remind us of just how smug and condescending he can be. It was Obama at his best: He made fun of the tastes of middle-class Americans, getting into hot water over a joke about how tacky…
articles.body:
With just over a week to go until the midterm elections, former President Obama joined the campaign trail to remind us of just how smug and condescending he can be. It was Obama at his best: He made fun of the tastes of middle-class Americans, getting into hot water over a joke about how tacky the Cheesecake Factory is. He also bemoaned how divisive our politics has gotten — while of course slamming his political opposition as utterly indecent.

What’s more, he reverted to his trademark gaslighting. It’s almost as if we were all back in 2012.

The comments came over the weekend at campaign stops in Ohio and later in Michigan, where the Democratic nominee, Abdul El-Sayed, is struggling with Black voters. El-Sayed’s efforts to court this traditionally stalwart Democratic bloc have fallen flat; a recent poll had former House Intelligence Chairman Mike Rogers (R-Mich.), the Trump-endorsed Republican candidate, picking up an unprecedented 33 percent of the Black vote.

Hence Obama’s appearance — a Hail Mary attempt to revive El-Sayed’s support with Black voters.

At the rally, Obama compared questions about El-Sayed’s connections to the Muslim Brotherhood to the Birther movement — the kooky conspiracy theory that Obama had not been born in the U.S.

“They will use lies, and maybe your name or your faith to somehow suggest you are dangerous and less American than they are,” he said . “We have seen this movie before. I starred in it! I’ve got a long-form birth certificate to prove it. This stuff didn’t work on me in Michigan, it’s not going to work on Abdul.”

But here’s the difference between the racist Birther movement and the questions about El Sayed: The claim that Obama wasn’t born in the U.S. was false, whereas the claim that Abdul El-Sayed has close ties to the Muslim Brotherhood is true.

Sayed’s mother is supposed to have worked for the Muslim Brotherhood. His sister bragged about it online , long before he was a candidate for anything.

El-Sayed himself signed a letter supporting the Muslim Brotherhood Egyptian leader Mohamed Morsi in 2012. The letter called on Morsi, then Egypt’s president, to purge his opposition from that nation’s police and media. At a time when American journalism and human rights non-profits were calling on Morsi to stop arresting and prosecuting journalists, El-Sayed signed a letter calling for an acceleration .

When confronted during this campaign, El-Sayed has refused to answer questions about it — instead berating the journalists who dare to ask them .

Obama wants to suggest that asking questions about any of this is racist, but it isn’t. Nor is it Islamophobic to ask a Muslim why he signed a letter supporting a group currently designated by multiple countries , in whole or in part, as a terrorist organization . To suggest that this somehow impugns all Muslims is to suggest that all Muslims support terrorism — which is, ironically, the actual racist position. Don’t forget: The people El-Sayed was calling to be purged by the Morsi regime were also Muslims.

No one has a problem with El-Sayed’s religion. A lot of people have a problem with the fact that he has a problem denouncing terrorists — something not true of most American Muslims.

The analogy with the racist Birther movement against Obama is equally fallacious. Saying someone’s not American because he is Black is racist. But calling someone racist for asking legitimate questions about someone running for office who cannot condemn Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps is not. It is not racist to question someone seeking office why he thinks Israel is an enemy equivalent to Iran, or why he would campaign with Hamas-lovers like Hasan Piker.

To say otherwise is just the purest form of woke gaslighting.

And Obama went further. He suggested that there is nothing at all radical about El-Sayed — as if the whole thing were just a psy-op designed to fool you.

“What they’re doing, which is par for the course, is running all kinds of scary ads to make you think Democrats are radicals or communists or jihadists or the woke police,” Obama said. “We are not going to fall for that. … Abdul is fighting for change, real change. … He’s taking on politics and corrupt politics that only benefits people with enough money and power to game a broken system in Washington at your expense. I hear people say this is somehow radical. What is radical about that? Wanting everybody to have health care? How’s that radical? Wanting everybody to have a place to live that they can afford? How is that radical?”

Again, this is the purest form of Obama gaslighting. El-Sayed spent the primary campaigning with Hasan Piker, a man who said he would vote for Hamas and that America deserved 9/11.

El-Sayed constantly accused his main opponent in that primary, Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.), of having dual loyalties to Israel. He justified a terror attack that nearly killed 140 Jewish preschoolers by saying that “hurt people hurt people” to explain the would-be mass murderer’s motivations. El-Sayed talks about Israel as an adversary on the scale of Iran. And that is radical.

Comparing El Sayed’s truly divisive politics to Medicare for All — or worse, pretending that Medicare for All is the sum total of problematic views held by El Sayed — is a deeply dishonest effort by Obama to evade legitimate questions.

By the way, El-Sayed, the great advocate of Medicare for All has a wife with a private medical practice that doesn’t take Medicare — or any other insurance for that matter. It seems pretty radical to force on the nation a health care system your own wife opts out of because it isn’t profitable.

Obama frequently bemoans how divisive our politics has gotten. Yet he himself seems perfectly willing to stand by the most divisive politicians of our time. He’ll even demean you for having a problem with it.

We all want a less divisive politics. President Trump’s language is frequently divisive — and so is Obama’s, albeit in a more genteel, condescending tone. No one wants to be the first to lay down their weapons.

Batya Ungar Sargon is the host of “ Batya !” which airs Saturday nights at 7 p.m. Eastern Time on NewsNation, the nation’s fastest-growing cable news network and a sister company of The Hill.

articles.title: Sen Slotkin threatened students like me. Senate needs an ethics probe
articles.summary: Sen. Elissa Slotkin faces ethics complaints after University of Chicago remarks about deterring young conservatives from government service.
articles.body: Michigan Senator Elissa Slotkin recently came to my campus, the University of Chicago, to join Vox editorial director Astead Herndon for a live program of America before a crowd of students. Believing she was speaking to a group of friends, she let her intentions be known should Democrats win back power in November. She wanted young conservatives interested in serving their country in its government to think, "Lord, that might be buying myself a ton of problems I don’t want, so let me avoid participating in that. I want that deterrence message sent." My friends and I received her "deterrence message," as did millions of patriotic Americans across the country. Unfortunately for Senator Slotkin, our team with the Chicago Thinker was there and listening to her every word. Now the walls are closing in. Members of Congress and President Trump have condemned her remarks. The Article III Project referred her to the Department of Justice’s Office of Civil Rights for inquiry and potential investigation. And a government watchdog filed an ethics complaint against her. Yesterday, I joined them by filing my own ethics complaint as the student reporter who originally broke the story. It’s time for the Senate Ethics Committee to open an investigation into Senator Slotkin for her remarks. The Ethics Manual is clear: "Conduct [that] has been characterized as ‘improper conduct which may reflect upon the Senate,’ … has provided the basis for the Senate’s most serious disciplinary cases in modern times." The question before the Committee, then, is whether threatening young conservatives would reflect poorly on the Senate and set a dangerous precedent for the future. SLOTKIN WANTS GOP PROSECUTIONS TO DETER YOUNG PEOPLE FROM TRUMP ADMINISTRATION JOBS It would. Senator Slotkin’s statement was clearly meant to intimidate one side of the aisle from serving their country in government by way of investigations and prosecutions. She did not merely send a deterrence message — she sent a threat to Americans who dare dissent from her liberal orthodoxy. Whatever your opinions of Senator Slotkin’s own politics, such threats are unbecoming of a member of the United States Senate. Senator Slotkin’s defense so far has been unconvincing. She claims all she really meant was that those who violate the law should be prosecuted for doing so. It’s hard to see how that’s the case when we reexamine her comments and put them in context. She wanted to send a "deterrence message" to those interested in serving in government, not to those interested in breaking the law. As the host remarked to her immediately after her comments, "You could make them a pariah socially, politically, maybe even legally," as she quietly nodded along in front of an audience of college students. If all she wanted to do was prevent those interested in breaking the law from joining the government, she could have said as much. But she did not. MIKE DAVIS: SEN SLOTKIN REVEALS HER INSIDIOUS SCHEME TO TARGET YOUNG CONSERVATIVES Let’s suppose the sides were reversed. Suppose a Republican senator said they would investigate and prosecute so many members of another’s staff that young public servants would be deterred from working for them out of fear of legal retribution. One can already imagine Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and his Democratic colleagues rushing to the Senate floor to condemn such comments and calling for an ethics investigation, censureship, or even expulsion. They would be right to do so, and I would join them in such calls. This is not about partisan games. Those who love this country, share its values and seek to serve it should be allowed — indeed, encouraged — to do so, no matter their political background. Many of our nation’s finest moments have come with the help of young staffers. Ted Sorensen began working as John F. Kennedy’s speechwriter when he was twenty-four. Peggy Noonan was in her early thirties when she did the same for President Reagan. And it was a team of young staffers, many in their twenties, who were dispatched in the Kennedy and Johnson administrations to document the oppression of Black Americans during the Civil Rights Era. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Should Senator Slotkin’s remarks go without formal condemnation from the Senate, or at the very least some form of investigation, I fear the consequences for our country. The world is rapidly changing. Artificial intelligence is shocking the economy, the global order and the minds of millions of Americans all at once. Wars rage on around the globe. Our body politic is more divided than at any point since the Civil War. Now is the time to be encouraging more political participation among our best and brightest youths, not less.

articles.title: Marijuana and violence: How much more evidence do we need of the connection?
articles.summary: Marijuana advocates have promoted the image of a harmless drug. Scientific research increasingly challenges this reassuring narrative.
articles.body:
For decades, marijuana advocates have promoted the image of a harmless drug producing relaxation, laughter, and peaceful behavior. That image has helped normalize marijuana use and fuel a multibillion-dollar commercial industry.

But scientific research increasingly challenges this reassuring narrative.

A major systematic review and meta-analysis published last month in the journal Psychological Medicine examined 63 studies involving more than 265,000 participants. Researchers found significant associations between marijuana use and violence across both general-population and psychiatric samples.

Among the general population, marijuana users had approximately twice the odds of perpetrating violence. Among psychiatric patients, the odds were nearly two and a half times as high.

The association with marijuana use was even stronger — 3.75 times as high in the general population — in studies examining violence resulting in criminal convictions. And among psychiatric patients, the association between marijuana and criminal violence was 4.21 times as high.

These findings deserve national attention, but this is hardly the first warning. A 2020 meta-analysis published in the American Journal of Psychiatry examined 30 studies involving nearly 300,000 adolescents and young adults. Researchers found that the odds a subject committed physical violence more than doubled if he was a marijuana user. Other studies have identified associations between marijuana use and intimate-partner violence .

Research involving patients with schizophrenia has raised additional concerns. The connection between marijuana, serious psychiatric illness, and violence is particularly troubling. Nearly four decades ago, a landmark 1987 study published in The Lancet followed 45,570 Swedish military conscripts over 15 years. Researchers found that those who had used marijuana more than 50 times had approximately six times the risk of developing schizophrenia compared with non-users.

Subsequent research has repeatedly associated marijuana consumption — particularly frequent use of high-potency products — with increased risks of psychosis.

Why does this matter when discussing violence? Schizophrenia and other psychotic disorders can involve paranoia, delusions, impaired judgment, and distorted perceptions of threats.

A 2009 meta-analysis published in PLOS Medicine found that schizophrenia and other psychoses were associated with increased violence risk, particularly when accompanied by substance abuse. The odds of violence were approximately twice as high without substance abuse but nearly nine times as high when substance misuse was also present. Although that analysis examined substance abuse broadly rather than marijuana alone, it highlights a potentially dangerous intersection of psychiatric illness and drug consumption.

Importantly, most people with schizophrenia are not violent . Nevertheless, the combined research raises questions about marijuana’s contribution to psychiatric vulnerability and behavioral risk. The scientific evidence does not establish that marijuana causes every violent incident involving its users.

Alcohol, other drugs, psychiatric conditions, and social circumstances may contribute as well. But uncertainty about causation is no justification for dismissing repeatedly observed risks.

Public-health authorities routinely warn consumers about potential dangers before every biological mechanism has been conclusively established. Why should marijuana receive different treatment?

There is another troubling dimension receiving far too little attention: The consequences of violence are not confined to marijuana users. They often fall upon spouses, intimate partners, children, neighbors, strangers, police officers, and emergency responders. Yet marijuana commercialization is frequently discussed as though its consequences were simply a matter of personal preference.

We hear about consumer freedom, business opportunities, employment, and government tax receipts. We hear almost nothing about the potential costs associated with violence, psychiatric emergencies, impaired driving , addiction , and family disruption. Those costs do not disappear just because they are difficult to measure. They are absorbed by victims, families, hospitals, employers, insurers, law enforcement, and taxpayers.

While marijuana businesses collect revenue from increasingly potent products, the public bears costs never appearing on the industry’s balance sheet. The new research does not establish how much violent crime marijuana directly causes or whether legalization increases violent crime. Those questions require additional investigation. But the findings reinforce a serious public-health concern that can no longer be dismissed as an isolated observation.

Public-health agencies should inform consumers about these associations. Medical professionals should assess marijuana use when evaluating psychiatric and behavioral problems. Policymakers should examine potential social costs rather than focusing exclusively on tax revenue.

A drug does not become harmless because it is legal, profitable, or socially fashionable. For years, Americans have been assured that marijuana’s consequences are largely limited to individuals choosing to consume it. The scientific research presents a considerably more troubling picture. The warning signs have accumulated for decades. How much more evidence will it take before public health officials, lawmakers, and the marijuana industry acknowledge the warning signs?

Scott Chipman is vice president of Americans Against Legalizing Marijuana .

articles.title: Jackson, Collins separated by 2 points in Maine Senate race polling
articles.summary: Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) is locked in a tight race against her Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson, according to a new survey. The Marist University poll, released one week before the midterms, found the incumbent trailing Jackson by 2 percentage points among likely voters in the state — a lead that falls within the survey’s margin…
articles.body:
Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) is locked in a tight race against her Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson, according to a new survey.

The Marist University poll , released one week before the midterms, found the incumbent trailing Jackson by 2 percentage points among likely voters in the state — a lead that falls within the survey’s margin of error.

Other recent polling has supported “toss-up” ratings for the race from election handicappers, like the Cook Political Report .

Another survey, released last week by Fox News, showed the two candidates tied in their support from likely voters in the state, while a Suffolk University poll conducted earlier this month similarly found the Democrat with a 2-point advantage.

Collins is running for a sixth term in Congress. If she is successful in the general election, she will become the longest-serving senator in the state’s history. Despite Jackson’s lead in the Marist poll, 58 percent of respondents said they believe the Republican will win.

Jackson, a logger and former state senator, also recently received the support of more than 60 former diplomats and top foreign affairs experts in his effort to oust the incumbent. The Democrat struggled to gain name recognition after replacing former Democratic nominee Graham Platner in the race.

The pollster also asked respondents to weigh in on the candidates in the state’s gubernatorial contest to replace Gov. Janet Mills (D). GOP nominee Bobby Charles and Democratic nominee Hannah Pingree were tied at 44 percent support in the survey among likely voters. Roughly 6 percent of respondents also backed the independent candidate in the race, Maine Sen. Rick Bennett.

Additionally, 58 percent of likely Maine voters disapproved of President Trump’s handling of his job as president. Forty-two percent of likely voters said Trump would not be a factor in how they cast their ballot this election, while 41 percent said their vote will be cast “against the president.”

The Marist University poll was conducted among 1,449 Maine registered voters from Oct. 22-25. It has a margin of error of 6.6 percentage points.

articles.title: The Movement: Israeli election could bridge widening gap within GOP
articles.summary: Voters in Israel are going to the polls Tuesday, in the first election since the Hamas terrorist attacks on Oct. 7, 2023. The contest is high stakes for Israeli citizens, who have a chance to weigh in on incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s handling of national security around the tragedy and his leadership in the…
articles.body:
Voters in Israel are going to the polls Tuesday, in the first election since the Hamas terrorist attacks on Oct. 7, 2023.

The contest is high stakes for Israeli citizens, who have a chance to weigh in on incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ’s handling of national security around the tragedy and his leadership in the subsequent wars. But it’s also a pivotal moment for Israel’s backers in the U.S., especially younger Republicans, who have diverged in recent years from their older peers when it comes to supporting Netanyahu.

That divide is even showing up in the White House, where President Trump endorsed Netanyahu last week, but Vice President Vance declined to do so. That suggests Vance is hoping to distance himself from the Trump-Netanyahu alignment, which helped to nudge the U.S. into the Iran war. Other isolationist conservatives, like Tucker Carlson and Steve Bannon , have turned to openly criticizing Netanyahu and the U.S.-Israel relationship.

Earlier estimates showed a tight race between Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot , former head of the Israeli Defense Forces. Official results will be published Wednesday.

Analysts say that while the outcome likely won’t change much about Israel’s policy in Gaza or Iran, a new personality atop the government could smooth U.S.-Israel relations in the eyes of young conservatives, many of whom have soured on Netanyahu in recent years.

Justin Logan , director of defense and foreign policy studies at the Cato Institute, said the difference between Trump and Vance reflects a generational divide in the GOP over Israel, broadly, and Netanyahu more specifically.

“I would say pretty much everybody on the right under 50 or so, who isn’t really strongly invested in Israel qua Israel, is sort of exhausted of the Middle East, is sort of exhausted of wars in the Middle East, didn’t understand the case why we attacked Iran in February of this year, and is sort of averse to deep involvement in the Middle East,” said Logan. “Whereas I think it’s a very boomerish inclination to say, you know, ‘Israel’s our greatest ally. We need to back them up on all their various endeavors in the Middle East.’”

Driving the schism, Logan and others said, is a growing tendency among younger Republicans to be isolationists. Those conservatives grew up around marathon wars in Iraq and Afghanistan and now want U.S. resources to be directed at domestic problems, rather than those around the world.

That isolationist streak doesn’t necessarily signal an erosion in support for Israel’s right to exist, he added. Generally, more Republicans of all ages have a favorable view of Israel than an unfavorable one. But among those under 50, 57 percent have an unfavorable view , according to Pew data from earlier this year.

That divide could be bridged by a new standard bearer for the Israeli regime. Trump has largely aligned himself with Netanyahu, especially since the Iran War. But as Trump’s time in office wanes, the new generation of Republicans is looking to throw that general support for Israel toward someone else.

“In American politics it’s complicated because Israel is popular in certain circles on the right in particular, and so people kind of hold Netanyahu up as an icon,” said Ben Friedman , policy director at Defense Priorities, a think tank focused on restraint-based foreign policy.

“But I think a lot of people, because of the way politics have shifted on Israel, would like to see a different prime minister of Israel, would like to see a government in Israel that creates less animosity in the base,” Friedman said. “Things might be easier if Netanyahu lost, I think, for a lot of people on the right.”

That dynamic does not necessarily go both ways. Joel Rubin , a former deputy assistant secretary of State under President Obama, said that because Trump is still broadly popular in Israel, the election is not likely to curb or change the Israeli government’s warmth toward him. And it could be a chance for Trump to make another run at brokering peace, since a non-Netanyahu government could be more open to moves that would soften relations with Israel’s Arab neighbors.

“If Trump is deft, he’ll end up likely still finding a lot of conversions and maybe even some more freedom of action with the Israelis who are open to, under Eisenkot, doing some things that Netanyahu currently isn’t in the West Bank and in Gaza that may help with some of the Arab states as well in the region,” said Rubin. “So I think Trump kind of comes out ahead in either direction on this one.”

In general, whoever wins the election is not likely to change Israel’s military strategy. Gone are the days of a left-wing party in Israel that supports a two-state solution with Palestine, or diplomatic detente with Iran, Friedman said. But a new regime could appear softer than the hawkish Netanyahu.

“The current Israeli government, I think, really exists on war — it’s like a coalition held together by conflict,” Friedman said. “So even if the left is not particularly dovish by normal standards, it’s going to be presumably less enthusiastic about continuing to bomb Iran as Netanyahu always pushes.

“I think their sort of dream scenario would be going back to peace,” he added, “not this sort of continual warfare that seems to be the model that Netanyahu wants, that Trump has bought into.”

RAMASWAMY SAYS AMY ACTON CAMPAIGN STARTED IT

Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican candidate for governor in Ohio, is doubling down on a controversial ad he released earlier this month that features the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent, Amy Acton, calling Acton a liar.

That ad has since garnered bipartisan blowback because it touches a sensitive note in Acton’s childhood history. Her birth mother, Donna Arthur , stayed married to Acton’s stepfather even after he was charged with sexually abusing Acton when she was 12 years old. The younger Acton has not spoken to or seen Arthur in many years.

The incumbent governor, Republican Gov. Mike DeWine , called the ad “deeply troubling” and urged Ramaswamy’s campaign to take it down. Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) , who is in a tight Senate race, said he would not have run such an ad. Trump and Vance have both stood by it.

Ramaswamy is offering no apologies, defending the ad and expanding its reach with millions of dollars in ad buys. Now he’s offering a new twist, saying Acton started it with the personal attack ads. He said on Fox News on Sunday that Acton had first used his own mother in an attack ad against him.

“I’ll tell you the advice I was raised in: You never start a fight, but if you find yourself in one, you finish it, and you have to stand for what is right and what is true,” Ramaswamy said. “They’ve attacked me. They’ve defamed my mother to media silence. It’s unbelievable. And yet, at the same time, they’ll trot out anything to attack a Republican.”

The Acton campaign did publish a press release in August going after Ramaswamy for hiring his own mother at the biotech company he founded and then touting her research about an Alzheimer’s drug — which later failed clinical trials — to raise the company’s stock price. A nonpartisan fact checker, PolitiFact, found that the Acton campaign’s claims that Ramaswamy “pushed a drug that he knew didn’t work” and “made hundreds of millions of dollars scamming people” were “ mostly false .”

Trump said the election in Brazil, in which the incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva defeated right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro , was “another rigged election.” Bolsonaro is the son of Jair Bolsonaro , the former leader who was close with Trump. More here .

Rep. Mike Lawler (R-N.Y.), who is in a tough reelection race, took a page from Trump’s book by hitting the McDonald’s drive-thru circuit. He was seen serving customers at a McDonald’s in Haverstraw, telling one “the extra SALT is in the bag,” a reference to the state and local tax (SALT) deduction cap he pushed to raise last year. Video here .

A group of Catholic bishops issued a statement saying they regret a White House photo op with Trump after a meeting last week. The bishops said they had expected the meeting to be private until the White House quickly released photo and video on social media. More here .

November 10-12: Conservative groups including Heritage, The Claremont Institute and the Conservative Partnership Institute gather at The Forum, a new national conference for conservatives featuring a range of speakers, including Scott Jennings , James Braid , Nick Freitas and Spencer Pratt . Details here .

November 18: The Foundation for Research on Equal Opportunity hosts Freedom & Progress 2026, a gathering of leaders committed to expanding opportunity through free enterprise, innovation, pluralism, and individual liberty. Details here .

articles.title: Days will get way shorter in November: How much daylight we’ll lose
articles.summary: We’re about to have fewer daylight hours as the calendar flips to November.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – With daylight saving time coming to an end this weekend , many of us are about to see our latest sunsets until February. In some parts of the country, the last sunset at 6 p.m. or later will happen before our clocks even fall back.

Our clocks being set back an hour early Sunday morning will, of course, cause early sunsets. That’s the trademark of standard time , shifting sunlight toward the morning and away from the evening.

But the natural tilt and orbit of Earth as we glide toward winter are also contributing to days feeling shorter , at least in terms of the sunlight we get to experience.

As part of that, many in the U.S. recently had their final sunset after 6 p.m. until well into 2027. Nashville, Tennessee, saw sunsets shift into the 5 o’clock hour over the weekend, while Providence, Rhode Island, last saw a sunset after 6 p.m. on Oct. 17. New York City and Panama City, Florida, will see their final 6 o’clock sunset on Monday, while Birmingham, Alabama, will make the shift on Tuesday.

More than 40 cities analyzed by Nexstar will have their final 6 o’clock sunset on Halloween, the night before clocks fall back an hour. For most of those cities, the sun won’t set after 6 p.m. again until February.

Five cities will see later sunsets before then. Tampa , Florida, for example, will see its first 6 p.m. sunset on January 19. Others set to see their days end later in January include Austin, Louisville, Indianapolis, and Knoxville, Tennessee.

Another 16 cities have to wait until daylight saving time starts again in March to experience a sunset later than the 5 o’clock hour.

Days are about to get way shorter in November, too.

Between Nov. 1 and Nov. 30, most cities will lose between 40 and 60 minutes of daylight. Chicago, for example, will lose 59 minutes of daylight next month, falling from about 10 hours and 20 minutes of daylight on Nov. 1 to less than nine hours and 25 minutes by Nov. 30.

Bismarck, North Dakota, is set to go from about 10 hours of daylight at the start of the month to less than nine by the end.

The table below shows how much daylight 62 U.S. cities stand to lose in November:

The U.S. nearly skipped changing the clocks in November after the House passed the Sunshine Protection Act, sending it off to the Senate with support from President Trump. But the Senate adjourned without taking any action on the permanent daylight saving time bill, and isn’t expected back until after Election Day. (The legislation doesn’t have a “clear path forward,” though, according to Senate Majority Leader John Thune.)

Several of our Canadian neighbors will not set their clocks back this weekend after they enacted permanent daylight saving time this year.

Clocks in the U.S. won’t “spring forward” until March 14, 2027.

articles.title: Will Trump contest the midterm election results?
articles.summary: As the 2026 midterms approach, concerns are mounting over whether President Trump will attempt to overturn results through legal challenges, seizure of voting machines, or other controversial measures.
articles.body:
State officials and millions of Americans are holding their collective breath, fearing that a sweeping Democrat victory in the coming midterm elections will prod President Trump to challenge the results in several states. The question is how far would he or could he go.

Trump has already ordered the Justice Department to deploy 1,000 “election monitors” to polling sites around the country. Attorney General Todd Blanche defended the move , claiming Trump “is doing the same thing that every single administration has done in our generation.”

But Trump has still never accepted the results of the 2020 election. He has repeatedly claimed, with bogus evidence or none at all, that elections are rigged. So when it comes to monitoring elections, the public has good reason to doubt his motives.

Ironically, about the only people convicted of election interference after the 2020 election were Trump supporters.

Would Trump initiate Department of Justice lawsuits against certain states or cities if Republicans lose? He’s already begun.

Trump ordered Blanche to file a preemptive lawsuit to block certification of the Senate election in Alaska if incumbent Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan (R-Alaska) loses.

Alaska uses a multiparty ranked choice voting system, which allowed another candidate named Dan J. Sullivan to make it to the general election as a Republican, along with the incumbent Republican Dan S. Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola. Ranked choice is a bad way to run elections, but the U.S. Constitution says the “Times, Places and Manner of holding Elections for Senators and Representatives, shall be prescribed in each State by the Legislature thereof.” And the Alaskan Supreme Court has ruled that the alternative Dan Sullivan cannot be removed from the ballot.

Democrats may have put the alternative Dan Sullivan on the ballot to confuse voters, but filing a preemptive challenge sets a terrible precedent that will encourage Democrats to follow suit once they control the White House again.

Would Trump confiscate voting machines in certain states or cities? He has done that, too.

Trump has confiscated voting machines and ballots in Puerto Rico, Atlanta and Arizona, looking for evidence that Democrats or foreign actors conspired to defeat him in the 2020 election. And yet, he has produced no evidence that any of those machines altered votes.

But that won’t necessarily stop Trump from claiming he found evidence of fraud, illegal aliens voting or vote tampering in the 2026 election, especially in blue states.

If Trump decides to seize voting machines, that action would disrupt the machines’ chain of custody. Once voting machines are out of state officials’ hands, they may be reluctant to certify election results. What might happen after that is anybody’s guess.

And then there’s this question: Would Trump call out the military if election results go against the GOP? Some of his associates recommended that action in the aftermath of the 2020 election, and he reportedly gave it serious consideration.

Some of the country’s top generals were apparently concerned that Trump would do just that. In a press conference in 2021 , former Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Mark Milley and former Secretary of Defense Lloyd Austin told the media “the United States military is an apolitical institution.” And they added, “We don’t arbitrate elections. That’s the job of the judiciary and the legislature and the American people. It is not the job of the U.S. military.”

The Trump administration recently denied it would deploy the military in case of a blue wave. But Trump told the New York Times last January that he regretted not ordering the National Guard to seize the voting machines in three swing states he lost in 2020. And Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth has already taken certain steps .

States have been organizing election-response and legal teams , filing their own lawsuits , and working to ensure nothing goes amiss. Trump may be less likely to challenge election results from red states, with the possible exception of Alaska, because it would embarrass those states’ Republican leaders who run the elections. Blue states are a different matter.

What if Trump does challenge the results of a few states? Would he demand Republicans in Congress refuse to recognize some newly elected Democrats? The Supreme Court has ruled the House of Representatives can’t exclude duly elected representatives unless the person doesn’t meet the Constitution’s qualifications. But the Trump-aligned Center for Renewing America claims democratic socialists cannot truthfully take the oath of office and outlines a newly released process for the House to exclude them.

Such efforts, if they were to happen, would likely turn voters against Republicans for years to come — unless Republicans finally stand up to Trump.

People occasionally rush to predict a “constitutional crisis” when the country hits a road bump. But if Trump refuses to accept the election results and takes questionable steps to challenge them, that really could lead to a constitutional crisis.

Merrill Matthews is the Texas state chair of Our Republican Legacy.

articles.title: Democratic senator: Trump is ‘laying the groundwork’ to steal Minnesota election
articles.summary: Retiring Sen. Tina Smith (D-Minn.) says that President Trump is “laying the groundwork” for MAGA allies to “steal” the Senate election after Trump said the federal government would be keeping an eye on the state. “He’s blatantly laying the groundwork to steal an election if his chosen candidate doesn’t win… Minnesota will not take kindly…
articles.body:
Retiring Sen. Tina Smith (D-Minn.) says that President Trump is “laying the groundwork” for MAGA allies to “steal” the Senate election after Trump said the federal government would be keeping an eye on the state.

“He’s blatantly laying the groundwork to steal an election if his chosen candidate doesn’t win… Minnesota will not take kindly to thinly veiled threats from a guy we’ve rejected three times (soon to be four),” Smith posted on the social platform X .

The senator made the comment in response to Trump’s warning that his administration is “watching closely” for voter fraud in the race between Republican Michele Tafoya and Democrat Peggy Flanagan to fill Smith’s seat.

“Let’s all get behind Michele Tafoya in Minnesota. She’s running a great race. Don’t allow them to play with the Votes after the race is over,” the president posted to Truth Social on Monday. “The Federal Government will be watching closely.”

“The only way she can lose is if they cheat by playing games with the Ballots as they come in,” he added.

Trump claimed without evidence he would have won Minnesota in the 2016, 2020 and 2024 presidential races if votes had been counted properly.

“We can’t allow that to happen, because I won Minnesota three times, but they didn’t give me the Victories, and Minnesota hasn’t been ‘won’ since 1972, when Richard Nixon claimed the trophy,” the president continued, referring to the last time a Republican candidate carried the North Star State in a presidential election.

Recent polls show the Senate race between Tafoya and Flanagan, the lieutenant governor, has tightened amid Republican criticisms over Democratic Gov. Tim Walz’s handling of widespread fraud within Minnesota’s social services programs that bilked hundreds of millions of taxpayer dollars.

Tafoya in a recent ad describes herself as a “pro-choice Republican” who’s “not afraid to stand up to my party” and slams Flanagan as a politician who “put politics first and let fraudsters steal your money.”

Another spot from the GOP hopeful accuses the Democrat and Walz of creating a “culture of corruption” in Minnesota.

Flanagan is running on affordability and has run ads touting “Medicare for All” and ending “Trump’s tax breaks for billionaires.”

She said in one recent ad that she is “running for Senate to help people afford their lives” and warned that Tafoya would be “another senator for Trump.”

Recent polls show Flanagan leading Tafoya by an average of 3.5 percentage points, according to RealClearPolling.com.

articles.title: Trump approval ticks up to 32 percent: Survey
articles.summary: President Trump’s approval rating inched up by 1 point from a record low last week, according to a new poll. The Reuters/Ipsos survey, released Monday, found 32 percent of U.S. adults support the president’s job performance, while 66 percent disagreed. This is a slight uptick from the pollster’s previous findings, which showed Trump with a…
articles.body:
President Trump’s approval rating inched up by 1 point from a record low last week , according to a new poll.

The Reuters/Ipsos survey , released Monday, found 32 percent of U.S. adults support the president’s job performance, while 66 percent disagreed. This is a slight uptick from the pollster’s previous findings, which showed Trump with a low 31 percent approval rating.

Rising costs amid the Trump administration’s ongoing war against Iran and trade battles with economic allies like Canada have strained the president’s public approval ratings.

These numbers have cast a shadow over Republicans’ prospects in the upcoming midterm elections, in which Trump has repeatedly urged Americans to vote as if he were on the ballot.

“I’m asking you to pretend that I’m on the ballot,” the president told a crowd of supporters at the GOP’s September midterm convention in Dallas.

“Just one more time, because if we lose, you’re going to lose your border, you’re going to lose your tax cuts, you’re going to lose your safety and security, you’re going to lose your wealth,” he added at the time.

Trump also promised during his speech to send $5,000 to each U.S. adult if Republicans hold control of both the House and Senate next year.

Before the onset of the Iran conflict on Feb. 28, respondents in Reuters/Ipsos polls displayed a preference for Republicans over Democrats when handling economic issues. In the latest survey, 37 percent of voters said Democrats had a better approach to the economy, while 33 percent said they would turn to Republicans on this issue.

The GOP is also seeking to close an enthusiasm gap ahead of the Nov. 3 elections, with the president traveling to stump for candidates in battleground states like Texas and Georgia. Some Senate Republicans warned that Trump’s presence is endangering vulnerable GOP candidates’ support from independent voters.

The latest poll found that more Democratic voters were excited to vote in the election. Around 46 percent of surveyed Democrats said they were “very enthusiastic” about casting their ballot, while only 30 percent of GOP voters said the same.

Additionally, 47 percent of respondents broadly favored Democrats over the 36 percent who supported Republicans on a generic ballot ahead of the midterm elections, the data shows.

The Reuters/Ipsos poll was conducted among 1,679 U.S. adults from Oct. 22 to 26. It has a margin of error of 2 percentage points.

articles.title: Neil Young sues Trump over Ohio rally song
articles.summary: Neil Young says President Trump’s fundraising committee is breaking a vow that “it would never again use ‘Rockin’ in the Free World’” at a campaign rally, and the musician is filing a $10 million copyright infringement lawsuit. The “Heart of Gold” singer filed the suit against the Trump 47 Committee on Monday. In the filing,…
articles.body:
Neil Young says President Trump’s fundraising committee is breaking a vow that “it would never again use ‘Rockin’ in the Free World'” at a campaign rally, and the musician is filing a $10 million copyright infringement lawsuit.

The “Heart of Gold” singer filed the suit against the Trump 47 Committee on Monday. In the filing, Young alleges that his 1989 hit was played just before Trump took the stage at a Youngstown, Ohio, rally on Oct. 12.

The lawsuit described the tune as a “blistering anthem that contrasts the hollow promises of American political rhetoric with the harsh realities faced by the poor, homeless and forgotten.”

“The lyrics paint vivid street-level portraits — a mother discarding her baby, addicts lost in despair, garbage piling in the shadows of prosperity — while the repeated chorus delivers a savage irony, celebrating freedom that clearly isn’t shared by all,” according to the filing.

The song, the complaint said, is “the opposite of everything that Donald J. Trump stands for.”

It’s not the first time that the 80-year-old songwriter has objected to the use of his music by the Trump campaign, first filing a copyright infringement lawsuit in 2020.

According to Young’s latest complaint, Trump’s reelection campaign “asserted no defense and immediately settled shortly after it was served, promising that it would never again use ‘Rockin’ in the Free World’ without a license and permission from Young.”

Young wrote in a 2018 message on his website that he first requested Trump stop using his songs at campaign appearances in 2015.

“I asked him then, in a widely shared, public letter to cease and desist,” Young wrote at the time.

“However, he chose not to listen to my request,” he added, “just as he chooses not to listen to the many American voices who ask him to stop his constant lies, to stop his petty, nasty name calling and bullying, to stop pushing his dangerous, vilifying and hateful rhetoric.”

articles.title: Manchin: Atmosphere right for ‘complete tsunami’ in midterms
articles.summary: Former Sen. Joe Manchin (I-W.Va.) said the midterms are trending toward being a “complete tsunami” ahead of the November elections where the GOP is projected to lose the majority in the House. “Well, the atmosphere is definitely right, I believe, for a complete tsunami,” the former senator said, responding to a question from Blake Burman…
articles.body:
Former Sen. Joe Manchin (I-W.Va.) said the midterms are trending toward being a “complete tsunami” ahead of the November elections where the GOP is projected to lose the majority in the House.

“Well, the atmosphere is definitely right, I believe, for a complete tsunami,” the former senator said, responding to a question from Blake Burman on NewsNation, The Hill’s sister station. “Cost of living is everything right now.”

A new AP/NORC poll found around 80 percent of respondents said they believed lawmakers should make lowering prices one of their highest priorities in the 120th Congress.

“People in West Virginia are having a hard time, grocery prices are out of sight, gasoline prices are out of sight, and we’re in a rural state. Rural states basically drive a long way to take care of your jobs and take care of your family,” Manchin continued.

“And with all of the things working, all the winds blowing against people, having any type of a quality of life now, just struggling,” he said. “And the president’s kind of nonchalant talking about things that basically doesn’t seem to resonate or connect.”

When asked what races Democrats are likely to win in states that President Trump carried in his 2024 presidential bid, Manchin first referenced races in Ohio and North Carolina.

He said he believed Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy will “pay a price in Ohio” for a recent controversial ad his campaign released regarding his opponent Democrat Amy Acton, showing her estranged mother calling her a “liar.”

“In North Carolina, Roy Cooper has definitely looked like he’s going to win it,” Manchin said.

An Elon University poll of the North Carolina Senate race found 52 percent of respondents favored former Gov. Roy Cooper (D), while the GOP’s Michael Whatley only received 39 percent backing.

Manchin has campaigned this election cycle with Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), who is the only Republican running for reelection in a state where former Vice President Kamala Harris won in 2024. He endorsed Collins in September and has even encouraged the sitting senator to leave the GOP to become an independent.

articles.title: Democrats hold 8-point advantage 1 week before midterms: Survey
articles.summary: Democrats have an 8-point lead over Republicans in the final week before the midterm elections, according to a new survey released Tuesday. The Marist Poll, conducted alongside NPR and PBS News, found voters favor Democrats over Republicans by 52-44 precent. Independents also prefer Democrats over the GOP, with 52 percent saying so. Another 39 percent…
articles.body:
Democrats have an 8-point lead over Republicans in the final week before the midterm elections, according to a new survey released Tuesday.

The Marist Poll , conducted alongside NPR and PBS News, found voters favor Democrats over Republicans by 52-44 precent.

Independents also prefer Democrats over the GOP, with 52 percent saying so. Another 39 percent of independents said they are likely to vote for Republicans, the poll shows.

Just over half of respondents at 51 percent said they think the Democrat running in their district will win, and 46 percent said the same about their district’s Republican candidate.

The pollsters also found that 44 percent of respondents said they will use their vote for Congress as a referendum against President Trump, while 21 percent say their votes will be in favor of the president. Roughly 35 percent say Trump has no role in their decision on who they vote into Congress.

Pollsters also found that 44 percent of independents said they will vote against the president, compared to 12 percent who said their vote will be in his favor.

A majority of voters say they are enthusiastic or very enthusiastic to vote in the midterms, at 84 percent. Another 16 percent said the opposite, the numbers show.

Just over 90 percent of Democrats are slightly more enthusiastic than the 86 percent of GOP voters who said the same. About 76 percent of independents say they’re excited to vote, according to the poll.

It also found that just over three-quarters of respondents, 77 percent, say they are confident that their state or local government will conduct elections fair and accurately, and 21 percent say they are not very confident or not confident at all about the results.

Democrats lead in believing local or state leaders will hold fair elections , at 88 percent, followed by 75 percent of independents and 68 percent of Republicans.

Most of the survey’s respondents say they think if their candidate loses, they should accept the election results, at 81 percent. Another 16 percent say their candidate should probably or definitely challenge the results.

Democrats and independents both said their candidates should accept the respective results of the elections, at 90 and 83 percent respectively. About 70 percent of GOP respondents agreed, according to the poll.

Trump has hit the campaign trail across several red states as part of his final pitch to voters to back Republicans on the ballot next Tuesday. The president has seen his approval rating drop in recent months over his handling of the economy , inflation , the Iran war and gas prices.

But the latest poll shows Trump’s approval rating to be at 40 percent, with 59 percent saying they do not approve of his handling of the presidency.

The NPR/PBS News/Marist survey was conducted Oct. 19-20 and included 1,289 respondents. The margin of error is 3.8 percentage points.

articles.title: Melania or the pope: Who brokered Russia-Ukraine ceasefire in Oleshky?
articles.summary: Competing claims over the ceasefire mark the latest tensions between the White House and the Vatican.
articles.body:
A critical localised ceasefire in Ukraine that promises to help more than 1,000 civilians has set off an unlikely contest over who brokered the truce.

The White House insists that United States’ First Lady Melania Trump mediated the ceasefire in Oleshky between Russia and Ukraine, after weeks of increasingly alarming reports from the town warning of a growing humanitarian crisis.

But the Vatican has offered its own narrative, suggesting that the pope was responsible for helping the pause in fighting through phone calls with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Here’s what we know about the Oleshky ceasefire, and why the diverging versions of what led to the truce matter:

Russia took the southern Ukrainian town of Oleshky in the Kherson region in the early days of the invasion in February 2022 and has retained control over it since.

But the town has suffered from extensive war damage and was later hit by flooding after the destruction of the nearby Kakhovka Dam in 2023.

According to residents and officials, those who remain in the town, which the US estimates at 1,700-2,000 residents, have reported severe shortages of food, medicine, and other supplies.

Then, on October 23, a brief ceasefire was announced. Ukrainian and Russian officials have said the pause in fighting over Oleshky will allow the delivery of humanitarian assistance and the evacuation of those who want to leave the Russian-occupied town.

They’ve added that humanitarian corridors would be established to allow for aid deliveries.

Both sides have said this ceasefire, which is scheduled to end on Sunday, is not a comprehensive end to hostilities. Multiple diplomatic efforts to end the war have so far failed.

Still, the Kremlin said on Monday that the truce might set a precedent for similar localised ceasefires in the future.

On Telegram, Russia’s Ministry of Defence announced that it had stopped shelling in the direction of Ukraine’s city of Kherson from 4am Moscow time (01:00 GMT) on Tuesday, to prepare for the effort in Oleshky.

“As head of the Ukrainian negotiating team, I confirm that the Ukrainian side is honouring its commitments,” Dmytro Lubinets, the parliamentary commissioner for human rights, said in a Facebook post confirming Russia’s timing of its halt.

What have Melania and the White House said?

Announcing the ceasefire on Friday, US First Lady Melania Trump said the situation in the town was “dire”, and it was on the “brink of disaster”.

“The people of Oleshky have limited electricity, live amid mined roads, and endure regular military attacks. It was abundantly clear that without my intervention, the possibility to bring humanitarian aid into the city and to evacuate the elderly would be impossible,” she said in a statement issued by the White House.

It added that Melania and her representatives had worked closely with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to define the terms of the ceasefire.

“Non-military, civilian leaders from both countries will work together to visit Oleshky residents in their homes and determine the level of assistance they require. Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine,” said Melania.

Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets also publicly thanked the first lady and her team for helping coordinate the talks. Russian officials confirmed the agreement.

The morning after the White House announcement, the Vatican published a front-page article in its official newspaper, L’Osservatore Romano. The headline: Humanitarian truce for Oleshky.

The article underscored that the ceasefire was secured after Pope Leo spoke to Russian and Ukrainian leaders, urging them to agree to the pause in fighting to help save trapped civilians.

Pope Leo spoke to Russian President Vladimir Putin via phone call on October 16 and expressed his “deep concern about the grave humanitarian situation in the city of Oleshky”, adding that he had called for a ceasefire to allow for food and medical assistance.

The pontiff made the phone call while he was in hospital recovering from surgery to remove a cancerous tumour in his lung.

Three days later, on October 19, Pope Leo also spoke with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy about the situation in Oleshky.

The pope’s special envoy, Cardinal Matteo Zuppi, had pressed Russian authorities on conditions in Oleshky during a visit to Moscow in late September.

Hasn’t Trump tussled with the pope before?

US President Donald Trump and Pope Leo have had a strained relationship.

Pope Leo, the first US pope in history, has criticised Trump’s decision to launch the Iran war, saying it violated Catholic moral principles of a “just war”.

In April, responding to Leo’s critiques, Trump said the pope was “weak on crime, weak on nuclear weapons”, and that he would not have been elected pope if Trump wasn’t president – claiming, without evidence, that his presidency had helped Leo into the position.

“Leo should get his act together as Pope, use Common Sense, stop catering to the Radical Left, and focus on being a Great Pope, not a Politician. It’s hurting him very badly and, more importantly, it’s hurting the Catholic Church!” Trump wrote on Truth Social at the time.

Does this matter for the US midterm election?

Among Catholics, Trump’s popularity is low. Refusing to even mention the pope’s role in the Oleshky ceasefire is unlikely to help him.

The midterms, scheduled for next week, often reflect a sitting president’s performance as voters decide whether Trump’s Republicans can retain control of Congress.

A Pew Research Centre study conducted between September 28 and October 4 suggested that Trump’s approval rating among Catholics has fallen from 47 percent at the start of his second term in January 2025 to just 30 percent in October 2026. As many as 20 percent of US adults identify themselves as Catholic.

Among white Catholics, Trump’s popularity has fallen from 59 to 39 percent, while among Hispanic Catholics it has crashed from 31 to 18 percent.

articles.title: Trump’s unforgivable legacy in Ukraine
articles.summary: As America celebrates its 250th anniversary of declared independence this year, citizens turn their thoughts to George Washington, Thomas Jefferson and … Benedict Arnold?
articles.body:
As America celebrates its 250th anniversary of declared independence this year, citizens turn their thoughts to George Washington, Thomas Jefferson and … Benedict Arnold?

Arnold, an ambitious young military officer in the Continental Army, won military victories for America that no one else had achieved, through his sheer tenacity and audacity to win — very much like President Trump’s assertive policies in his first term. But also like Trump, Arnold’s self-aggrandizement did not win the universal praise he craved. Others, whom he considered less worthy, received the recognition and honors he felt he alone deserved.

For Arnold, it was military promotions and rising career assignments; for Trump, it was perhaps the Nobel Peace Prize and re-election.

Both men became increasingly embittered on major national security issues against their own country and ultimately supported some of America’s major adversaries. Trump had been an admirer of strong, nondemocratic leaders even before suffering those perceived slights. Arnold became the new country’s first accused traitor , though he was never formally charged before he fled to England.

Trump has openly blamed Ukraine for starting and continuing the war that Russia started and continues.

Ukraine is a fellow democracy, an aspiring NATO ally already effectively defending NATO territory against further Russian aggression, and a loyal friend of the U.S. Yet Trump constantly disparages its cause, periodically cuts off vitally needed weapons and intelligence support and, with Vice President JD Vance, treats Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelensky, in a boorish and bullying manner . It is a vivid contrast to Trump’s openly ingratiating treatment of Russian dictator Vladimir Putin , who has perpetrated extensive war crimes in Ukraine — an embarrassingly demeaning posture for a U.S. president.

Given the obvious threat to NATO that a Russian victory over Ukraine would present, Trump’s increasingly open support for Putin’s invasion of Ukraine — which he once called “genius” and “savvy” — clearly endangers U.S. national security.

Trump has also repeatedly claimed that there wouldn’t have been a Russia-Ukraine war at all if he had been in office at the time. Presumably, he was referring to his close personal relationship with Putin. Does he mean he would have been able, and willing, to confront Putin and dissuade him from his aggressive intentions? Or, conversely, does he mean that he would have been able to discourage Ukraine from defending itself against the Russian onslaught by completely denying it U.S. arms, intelligence and diplomatic support to demonstrate the futility of resistance?

One reliable indicator of Trump’s real intentions is what he has done since returning to office and possessing America’s supreme military, economic and political powers to influence world events. In the six years of Trump’s presidency so far, he has made no visible effort to urge Putin to withdraw from Ukraine, on the basis of either personal respect and “friendship” or because of deference to American power under Trump.

Instead, Trump only mildly suggests that Russia advance no further in Ukraine and agree to a ceasefire in place. Zelensky has repeatedly accepted the U.S. proposal and even halted its attack on Russian refineries this month. While Ukraine held its fire for three days, Russia launched its greatest missile and drone onslaught of the war.

With Republicans poised to lose control of Congress, Trump could fear a revived impeachment effort, this time on the devastating grounds of aiding an enemy of an ally. The formal accusation would be devastating to his legacy.

Arnold escaped the jurisdiction of the states, which would have prosecuted treason at the time. His reputation, not unlike Trump’s, had already been tarnished. He was court-martialed by the Continental Army in 1779 for the non-treasonous charges of profiteering and misconduct.

Trump, through his actions, has made abundantly clear whose side he is on in Russia’s war on Ukraine. If he continues on his overt anti-Ukraine, pro-Putin course, he could well surpass Benedict Arnold’s shameful legacy.

Joseph Bosco served as China country director for the secretary of Defense from 2005 to 2006 and as Asia-Pacific director of humanitarian assistance and disaster relief from 2009 to 2010. He is a nonresident fellow at the Institute for Corean-American Studies, a member of the advisory board of the Global Taiwan Institute and member of the advisory board of the Vandenberg Coalition.
